*Granularity:*
	- required breakpoints
	- monthly
	- Gaussian Processes (absolute granularity)

*Level of assumptions*
	*- On seasonality:*
		- Anything model finds
		- Anything model finds, but constrained by breakpoints
		- Defined direction - coming from multiple-year research model
		- Defined direction - coming from attribution
		- Defined direction and quantities (bookkeeping)

* *On effect of ads*
** Everything goes to ads
  interpret differences in OS as change in Ads effectiveness
  potentially bigger effects on ads
  	=> helps relax assumptions on ads and can be partially more accurate therefore
  	=> ideally seasonality confirmed on previous years (but not if we assume there're also competitors)
  	=> confirming the seasonality and making it always happen is a separate burden
** Everything goes to Android/iOS change
  interpret differences in OS with no credit to ads
  potentially smaller effects



Basically, we have two options on how to use time-varying coefs:
*1) relax the assumptions of constant impact of ads:*
*Assume*: relation of Android and iOS is always same (tourists excluded). But ads change impact
*Requirement* - coefficients do not change drastically (hold them with hierarchical)
*Result*: potentially less systematic errors, probably more trustworthy weights (only if we trust the assumptions). Coefficients might be a bit inflated.
*Simplest* - monthly or periodic gradation. Complex - GPs


*2) adding some actual assumed seasonality*
*Assume*: the seasonality. And how it develops across the year
*Requirement* - seasonality holds across years and actually normalizes the error.
(*NOTE*: If we think it normalizes the error, than it actually also means there’s high chance it will be aligned with results of assumption relaxing)
*!!!* (We only accept the model if it improves fit or error normality, right?)
*Result* - using the seasonality for budgeting (increase/decrease budgets during the year).



*BUT:* Whenever we are extracting time-varying impact with model, we are anyway JUST INTERPRETING the difference (changing relations over time) between Android and iOS to ads. This difference could be coming from other places, but we are anyway just choosing to assign it to ads.

Reason for that is that we would only be accepting the models that would help our error be more like white noise and less systematic (since we do not have other non-experimental way to validate it).

Hello, team. there is update about this case, please? Thanks.

*Am I correct that matching policy helps to prioritize couriers with the matching policy for a specific provider even if the delivery would take a bit longer OR do I miss the point?*

* Yes BUT although it prioritizes couriers with the matching policy for a specific provider, for “premium quality” all merchants have this policy attached to them for it to work as intended. Basically the soft matching policies (in this case premium quality) apply a penalty to couriers without the policy, but couriers without the policy can still be assigned if their overall score, including the penalty, is better than couriers with the policy.

*What is the reason we need to prioritize couriers who would deliver longer?*

* The idea here is not to select couriers who would deliver longer. The northstar here is to assign less orders to couriers with poor performance i.e NOT have the premium matching policy so they get deprioritized. In a balance market, this might lead to slightly higher delivery time but we assign less and less orders to poor couriers eventually hoping they would churn from the platform and also vice versa assign more and more orders to good couriers so that they say loyal to the platform. It is our mechanism to prioritize good couriers when blocking poor couriers (mainly because of Acceptance Rate) is not allowed.

*Clarification needed here: ‘Meaning we don’t deprioritize couriers without the policy and they have a chance to be assigned’.*

* This means couriers without the matching policy are not completely excluded from being assigned to an order. Even if they lack a matching policy, they can still be assigned if their overall score, including the penalty, is better than other couriers with matching policies.

*Can you clarify why we state that we don’t deprioritize the ones without matching policy if, based on the example above, we would assign the order to the courier who would need 10 mins to deliver it if he has a matching policy instead of courier 2 who would deliver this in 8 mins but without the matching policy?*

* The couriers without the matching policy are not completely deprioritized because their penalty is only a small adjustment to their overall score. In cases where their location or other factors (e.g., delivery time) still make them a better option, they could still be assigned. However, in the example given, the penalty is enough to shift the preference towards a courier with the matching policy, even if that delivery takes a bit longer.

*What is the reason for this? : “If those couriers without policies stick in areas where we have a lot of couriers already, then there is a high chance that they will not be assigned orders”.*

* If there are many couriers in an area, those without matching policies are less likely to be assigned orders because there will likely be several couriers who have the matching policies and are also well-positioned for the delivery. The system will prioritize couriers with the policies, and in areas with many couriers, the ones without matching policies will have more competition and therefore less chances of being assinged an order.

*Do the couriers know that this premium policy is by default enabled for all of them when they register?*

* No, couriers are not informed that the premium policy is enabled for them by default.

*Is there a risk of communicating this? If yes, which one?*

* What do you mean? We don’t communicate this to couriers at all. This is an admin based feature.

*When we would remove premium policy “tag” for a courier, then would we notify them somehow about this or would there be any kind of other data based on what they could come to a conclusion that this policy has been removed from them?*

* No, couriers would not be notified if the premium policy "tag" is removed from them, and there would be no direct data visible to couriers that would allow them to conclude this. Unless they can anecdotally observe and come to this conclusion which is quite difficult.

*Is there a risk of communicating this? If yes, which one?*

* What do you mean? We don’t communicate this to couriers at all. This is an admin based feature.

*Do we assign this by default to all new couriers or do we select them based on their performance?*

* It depends on market to market.
* _Approach 1_

If we have a small % of couriers we want to prioritize from the entire list,  add "premium policy" to these already known couriers. They will be prioritized by the system to receive orders.

* _Approach 2_

If we have a large % of couriers we want to prioritize (in other words deprioritize small % of couriers), we add "premium policy" to all couriers except for the ones we want to  deprioritize. In this case, every new courier we add to funnel should also have this "premium policy" added to their profile.

*Do we assign this automatically by the system or is this local ops who do this?*

* I think local ops has to enable this feature in Admin

*Why do we want to remove it for low AR couriers? What would the time period be for this?*

* We want to remove it for Low AR couriers to prioritize them hoping they would eventually churn.

*What should AR be to remove the policy? The maximum AR is 100%?*

* Max is 100%. What should be the AR to remove policy also varies market by market. Some market want to depriroitzie all courier at 30% and below. Some only 20% and below. Some only 10% and below.

*Is this removal temporary until they increase their AR?*

* Technically yes, but in a realistic scenario, since we apply it to low AR couriers, it is very unlikely their AR would increase considerably for us to reconsider our decision. Also this is not an automatic procedure. We will manually have to assign them this tag if we think their AR has improved. Historically, no one has checked this so I doubt we reassign them this policy.

*If they do not receive orders due to this, how high is the chance they would be able to increase this within a reasonable period of time and not years?*

* They DO receive orders. The numbers of order they receive are less but they still receive orders. They can improve this over a week or a month. Depending on them entirely since AR is at an order level. If they start getting less orders but accept all of them their new AR would be 100%

*How much of income would they lose (approximately)?*

* I don’t know. No idea on this.

*Is this in all countries?*

* It’s not live anywhere except for PT and maybe HR.

*What else are we doing with low AR couriers? Do we block them if their AR drops lower?*

* Depends on market to market. In all Class 1 and some Class 2 markets we block them based on business needs.

Hello,

Unfortunately, the order’s payment state on the order page is not really accurate and only show if a payment capture request was sent, but does not specify if the payment was completed. 
Business products have their own platform which is quite different from the other verticals (Rides, Food, etc) making it hard for all the parties involved (Business, Billing, Fraud, Payments, Pricing, etc) to synchronise some information. 
The process in Commerce is that Billing receives order price data from Pricing team, then sends a request for payment to Payments team. Normally, for the other verticals, when an order payment fails, it should be added immediately to the next order made by the same account. But in the case of business account, due to the asynchrony I explained above, Billing might sent the request to recapture the failed payment with a delay that can be extended to year. The only team that can help understand better why the payment was retried only after 2 years would be Billing (if not assumed as a normal way of working by them).

Hey! This is quite ad-hoc as quite different scenarios are all labelled as "interim." My views below...*Formalised:* Job Change in Workday, potential change in job title, compensation and reporting lines, employment annex may be required dependent on country
*Not formalised:* Agreed additional responsibilities with manager, may receive some payment as OTP or acting up allowance if agreed, may notOther points:

* Maternity Leaver: Most volume here, approach varies on the market, in e.g. EE and RO, we typically backfill rather with perm due to long leave periods (~2 years), elsewhere we would typically hire an FTC rather than expand an existing employees remit for that period
* Interim cover for vacant role: This also happens quite a lot and tends to be approached with the formalised interim role route mentioned above.
* "Trying" out acting up for a period, this isn't so common, it typically starts as above (interim cover for vacant role) then the person's delivery when compared to external candidates may merit consideration for the permanent role.

We had a meeting to discuss the investigation into the cause of the deadlock. 

The primary issue was the use of the {{INSERT INTO ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE}} statement. 

The requests are coming from the message queue (MQ) and executing multiple requests concurrently across multiple connections, which leads to a concurrency race condition involving gap locks and next-key locks. This ultimately results in a deadlock, causing the first query to roll back.

While the developers have suggested using {{SELECT FOR UPDATE}}, the recommendation is to follow a simpler approach by separating the {{INSERT}} and {{UPDATE}} operations:

# Attempt to insert the value.
# If the insert fails due to a duplicate key constraint,
# Retry with an update statement.

This method should help reduce the occurrence of deadlocks.

* Answer
{noformat}Yes, I would expect TiDB to have similar deadlocks.
There is INFORMATION_SCHEMA.DEADLOCKS that should help with this.
Note that TiDB doesn't yet support SKIP LOCKED syntax.
See also: https://docs.pingcap.com/tidb/stable/troubleshoot-lock-conflicts#deadlock-errors
Note that one way of avoiding deadlocks is to always use the same order for locking and updating. There are many ways of doing this but SELECT...FOR UPDATE is one of them. While this would avoid deadlocks this would still have the same records being locked etc. which would result in transactions waiting on each other. Depending on how the application works you might be able to avoid this by changing how the data is stored.{noformat}

Profiling on the driver details

*Base query - NOT PROFILING READY*

{noformat}--------- //////////////////// -----
SELECT 
x.country_code,
sum(x.sum_total_problem_orders) AS sum_problems_eur,
approx_distinct(x.payout_id,0.0041) AS count_payouts,
approx_distinct(x.driver_id,0.0041) AS count_drivers
FROM 
(WITH stats AS(
		--
		SELECT
		co.driver_courier_id AS driver_id,
		date_trunc('week',co.created) AS week_stats,
			--(CASE WHEN co.created BETWEEN date('2023-10-29') AND date('2024-03-30') THEN co.created  + INTERVAL '3' HOUR ELSE co.created  + INTERVAL '4' HOUR END)) AS week_stats,
		co.country_code AS country_code,
		approx_distinct(co.order_id,0.0041) AS all_orders,
		round(COALESCE (sum(co.partner_price_eur),0),0) AS all_orders_sum,
		--
		--- INAPP VOLUME -----
		--
		round(COALESCE(sum(CASE WHEN co.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN co.partner_price_eur ELSE 0 END),0),0) AS sum_inapp,
		approx_distinct(CASE WHEN co.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN co.order_id ELSE 0 END,0.0041) AS count_inapp,
		-- FRAUD PROBLEM TOTAL 
		--
		round(COALESCE(sum(CASE WHEN co.driver_courier_fraud_label = TRUE OR co.is_chargeback = TRUE or co.propagated_chargeback = TRUE OR co.is_final_failed_payment = TRUE OR co.is_payment_problem = TRUE THEN co.partner_price_eur ELSE 0 END),0),0) AS sum_total_problem_orders,
		approx_distinct(CASE WHEN co.driver_courier_fraud_label = TRUE OR co.is_chargeback = TRUE or co.propagated_chargeback = TRUE OR co.is_final_failed_payment = TRUE OR co.is_payment_problem = TRUE THEN co.order_id END,0.0041) AS count_total_problem_orders,
		round(COALESCE(sum(CASE WHEN co.driver_courier_fraud_label = TRUE OR co.is_chargeback = TRUE or co.propagated_chargeback = TRUE OR co.is_final_failed_payment = TRUE OR co.is_payment_problem = TRUE THEN co.partner_price_eur ELSE 0 END)/NULLIF(sum(co.partner_price_eur),0),0),1) AS ratio_total_problem_sum,
		--
		-- DRIVER FRAUD 
		--
		sum(CASE WHEN co.driver_courier_fraud_label  = TRUE THEN co.partner_price_eur ELSE 0 END) AS sum_driver_fraud,
		approx_distinct(CASE WHEN co.driver_courier_fraud_label = TRUE THEN co.order_id END,0.0041) AS count_driver_fraud
		--
		FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders AS co
		WHERE co.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -14, CURRENT_DATE) AS date)
		AND co.order_type ='rides' AND co.order_state = 'finished'
		AND co.payment_method_group = 'in-app'
		GROUP BY 1,2,3
		),
		--
	iban AS 
	(
		SELECT 
		ca.country,
		ca.account_iban,
		approx_distinct(pc.external_id) AS count_drivers
		FROM ng_payout.invoicing_payment_client_account ca
		JOIN glue.ng_payout.invoicing_payment_client AS pc ON ca.client_id = pc.id
		WHERE ca.created_date >= date('2023-01-01')
		AND ca.account_iban IS NOT NULL
		AND ca.account_iban <> ''
		GROUP BY 1,2
		ORDER BY 3 DESC
	)
		SELECT
		DISTINCT pp.id AS payout_id,
				date_trunc('week',pp.created) AS created_week_payout,
				date_diff('day',s.week_stats,date_trunc('week',pp.created)) AS diff_created_sanity_check,
				s.week_stats AS created_week_orders,
				ca.country AS country_code,
				pp.client_id,
				pc.external_id AS driver_id,
				s.sum_total_problem_orders,
				s.ratio_total_problem_sum,
				s.all_orders_sum,
				pp.created_date AS creation_date_payout,
				pp.amount AS amount,
				pp.currency AS currency,
				round(pp.amount /r.rate,0) AS payout_eur,
				pp."method" AS method,
				pp.state AS state,
				pp."type" AS TYPE,
				ii.*,
				ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY pp.id ORDER BY pp.created DESC) AS rn
					FROM  glue.ng_payout.invoicing_payment_payout AS pp
					LEFT JOIN glue.ng_payout.invoicing_payment_client AS pc ON pp.client_id = pc.id
					LEFT JOIN glue.ng_payout.invoicing_payment_client_account AS ca ON pp.client_id = ca.client_id 
					LEFT JOIN glue.ng_public.vw_currency_exchange_rates r ON r.currency = pp.currency AND date(r.valid_on) = date(pp.created)
					LEFT JOIN stats AS s ON pc.external_id = s.driver_id 
					LEFT JOIN iban AS ii ON ca.account_iban = ii.account_iban
							AND
						--DATE(s.week_stats) = DATE(date_trunc('week',(pp.created + INTERVAL '24' HOUR)) - INTERVAL '7' DAY)
						--CASE WHEN ca.country = 'th' THEN s.week_stats = date_trunc('week',(pp.created + INTERVAL '24' HOUR)) - INTERVAL '7' DAY 
						---ELSE 
						s.week_stats = date_trunc('week',pp.created) - INTERVAL '7' DAY
						--END
		WHERE 
		pp."method" = 'regular'
		AND 
		pp."type" = 'ride_hailing_driver'
		AND
		pp.state = 'finished'
		--AND 
		--s.driver_id IS NOT NULL
		--AND
		--pc.external_id = 5489157
		--AND ca.country = 'th'
		--AND s.ratio_total_problem_sum > 0.5
		AND pp.created  >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -12, CURRENT_DATE) AS date)
		--AND date_diff('day',s.week_stats,date_trunc('week',pp.created)) > 7
		--AND round(pp.amount /r.rate,0) > 200
		ORDER BY 2 DESC) 
AS x 
WHERE x.rn = 1
AND x.count_drivers > 3
AND x.ratio_total_problem_sum > 0.5
GROUP BY 1


LIMIT 1000


		{noformat}

# +*Account changes/updates details:*+
## _Bank details last change_
While change of banking details on their own do not suggest fraud, it is a great indicator of (non-usual) activity on the drivers account. If we were to pair this with further order activity indicators, we can get a better picture of cases of 1) potential takeovers 2) potential selling 3) fake accounts.

Cases of more than half payout volume problematic with recent change of banking info (<7 days) as well as not a brand new driver (age > 14) cases have an annual impact of {color:#bf2600}*96K eur and 8K eur monthly*{color}.  *Recent noteworthy UK driver account hijacking cases were also picked up through these stats and stand for majority volume.* With the UK cases, we also need to consider the extra regulatory impact from payout out any sum to a third party.

{color:#ff5630}*The legal implications in both the UK and Ireland on blocking riders from using the platform are below:*{color}

*Contract Law:*

Both UK and Irish contract law require that any action taken by Bolt to block a rider must be in compliance with the terms and conditions that the rider agreed to when signing up for the platform.

As per the terms and conditions signed up by Rider in UK and Ireland (explained in detail in second question) a message may not always be required before suspending or blocking a rider’s account, especially in cases of severe breaches. However, the terms do mention actions like warnings in some cases but our internal process involves notifying the rider of any blocks or consequential actions taken. 

+*United Kingdom*+
The UK’s Consumer Rights Act 2015 regulates unfair terms in consumer contracts. There’s a requirement for fairness, transparency, and a balance of rights between the consumer and the business. 
+*Ireland*+
Consumer Protection (Unfair Terms) Regulations 1995: This Irish legislation, based on the EU Unfair Terms Directive, similarly protects consumers from unfair contract terms. 

This means that failing to explain why a rider was blocked could be considered unfair. As our terms do not explicitly have a requirement to notify and we notify as per our process, we must ensure the message for the block is clear.

h4. *Consumer Protection Laws:*


+*United Kingdom*+
Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations 2008: These regulations prohibit businesses from engaging in misleading or aggressive practices. Blocking riders without clear reasons, without warning, or in a way that could be considered unfair or deceptive, may violate these regulations.

+*Ireland*+
Consumer Protection Act 2007: This Irish law prohibits misleading, aggressive, and unfair commercial practices. Blocking a rider without sufficient explanation or transparency could fall foul of these provisions. Like in the UK, the company must avoid any practices that could be deemed unfair or misleading, such as ambiguous terms or arbitrary bans.

*We should confirm with the privacy team what the implications would be from GDPR and data protection perspective.* 

{color:#ff5630}*What obligations does Bolt have to riders? Does a message need to be sent to riders?*{color}

*Relevant Clauses under the Terms and Conditions:* Below are the relevant clauses under the Terms and conditions, in relation to blocking an notification:

[*Ireland Passenger Terms and Conditions:*|https://bolt.eu/en-ie/legal/terms-for-riders-2024/?category=rides]

* *Clause 2.8*: Bolt has the right to *suspend or close your account* if any of the information you provide is illegal or if your activities contravene Bolt's terms.
* *Clause 5.9*: Bolt may take action, including *suspension* of accounts for a period of 6 months if a rider repeatedly cancels rides within 24 hours​
* *Clause 8.3*: Bolt retains the right to *close a rider's account* without prior notice if they violate the terms, such as withholding payment or acting maliciously such as being disrespectful to drivers
* *Clause 5.5* mentions that Bolt may issue a *warning* and *temporarily block* accounts for successive cancellations before proceeding to longer suspensions​

h4. [*United Kingdom Terms and Conditions:*|https://bolt.eu/en-gb/legal/terms-for-riders/?category=rides]

* *Clause 7(d)*: Bolt may immediately *withdraw your right to use and access* the platform (temporarily or permanently) if you breach any part of the terms or policies, or if it is necessary to protect the safety of drivers​
* *Clause 7(e)*: Termination or suspension of the account may result in the *deletion of user content* and loss of access to the platform​.
* *Clause 7(d)(iii)* allows Bolt to *issue a warning* before taking stronger actions such as suspensions, but this is not obligatory depending on the severity of the breach​.

Bolt’s terms suggest that a message may not always be required before suspending or blocking a rider’s account, especially in cases of severe breaches. However, the terms do mention actions like warnings in some cases. However, the - current process for handling safety events in the UK&IE - here clearly mentions CS Safety agents are responsible for placing and communicating passengers' blocks. The user (passenger) must be informed if and for how long the account is suspended based on the information given in the Global Event Assessment Tool (screenshot attached for reference). In high priority cases, the app displays _“You have been blocked till further notice, check your in-app message for more details or contact support.”_ In case of hard blocking, to inform the user an email must be sent because they cannot access their Bolt messages.

!https://lh7-qw.googleusercontent.com/docsz/AD_4nXebUgvZpbXKoXIC9oOvYf91GRw5cE0uI82moiOoYTC6YcMcRvawGh89qKTl-LbwkmGZvjS6KwxMCzd_dawqy7T8sD8NzciGxIAm_Rp9618j4eCzfpRmPsXXaOExfOHNkgZZ9nxJJ5qV1r9Za4_OvJuppA2D?key=bUoCp83miNO58LqHnWuLzQ|width=1600,height=835!

Also, [+Safety: The Global Event Assessment Tool+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/x/gIAQ7], mentions that in case of any consequential actions taken, the decision should be communicated to the user (passenger) as per the Standard Operating Procedures and should be made aware of not acting in accordance with Bolt T&Cs and if this type of (repetitive) action occurs again, their account might be suspended or terminated.

!https://lh7-qw.googleusercontent.com/docsz/AD_4nXcshCFjsqVVp_lj0NT_Pq8TRSBqcT1J0O8Ci9zqRwMrFn3HeWgReKrW3v7n-y8azl2D6Yzz2jMZYhG8TsQZ5kRZX28DpeIsd_Edae65aYQ8O1t9qRAEJfTuoVWz_PeQ9gIJHTV2HYn9SsIlHnJInfbEfjM4?key=bUoCp83miNO58LqHnWuLzQ|width=1600,height=803!



{color:#ff5630}*Do riders need to be given the opportunity to appeal the decision?*{color}

Bolt's terms do not explicitly state a formal appeal process for riders who are blocked or suspended. However, riders have the opportunity to contact customer support through the app to dispute charges or report unsatisfactory experiences.

*Ireland (Clause 4.5)* and *UK (Clause 11)* both outline methods of resolving disputes, indicating that riders can contact Bolt for support​. While no specific mention is made of an appeals process, general dispute resolution mechanisms are available through the app.

Further, I did go through confluence pages and slack, there is no concrete document that states riders have the right to appeal. This document [+here+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/x/5YJk7] is a draft from 2022 on Blocking Support for Blocked Riders which was created to introduce an appeal form so riders will be informed about blocking and potentially deflecting them. However, it is clear we must notify the rider but there is no concrete evidence/page confirming riders right to appeal. Legally no right to appeal could be challenged on unfair terms.

I think we should confirm this with the business and share any pages. 
Happy to discuss in person.

4.9.5 - this is purely business decision whether we want to charge the Partner for delivery in the situation described. If not, feel free to remove “In such cases Bolt has the right to charge the Partner for the cost of the delivery”. You may want to clarify the general practice about such charges with other business stakeholders as I am not an expert on charges in these situations in different markets.

4.15 - 4.25 - their suggestions are not in line with our operations model. Couriers are not our employees and we cannot exercise control over them. We do prescribe some minimum requirements, but the more requirements we add the more we increase our reclassification risk. Couriers are required to comply with applicable legislation and if requirements listed by the partner are required by law - couriers will need to adhere. I will share the requirements with product legal counsels and they can conduct additional assessment on whether this is something we can add in the future.

5.5 - apologies, I must have missed it. The effective functioning of the Bolt Food Platform is not only dependent on Bolt, but a lot of other service providers (e.g. server providers), and therefore, we shouldn’t accept any amendment requests. However, this should be assessed on case by case basis for key players. In any case, Bolt’s liability should be limited in accordance with Section 12.2 (i.e. Bolt is not liable for any indirect damage or loss of profit). If this is fine from the business perspective then we can accept the change, but from legal side this change is not recommended as it extends our liability.

5.7 - this is not acceptable. If refunds policy is a concern, we can change the wording as we did in case of other partners - add refunds policy to Special Terms and then it can be amended only with the consent of both parties.

9.3 - then this wording should be fine.

13.6 - we cannot make changes dependent on their receipt of our communication - we roll out changes for everyone at the same time, so this is simply impossible in practical terms. The date on which new terms will come into effect will be displayed on our webpage. They will be able to reach out to us and agree on special terms that will be added as an annex to the Special Terms we will sign with them if both parties agree to these changes. Otherwise, if they refuse to accept our changes and we will not be able to accommodate their request - there will be no other solution than to terminate the agreement.

TLDR from [docs|https://www.dragonflydb.io/docs]:

Dragonfly is able to run in 2 modes - same like redis: standalone master/replica + control from Sentinel and Cluster.

[Standalone|https://www.dragonflydb.io/docs/managing-dragonfly/replication] acts same as Redis and can even support one way migration from Redis v6.2 to Dragonfly and supported by Sentinel.

Because it’s multi-threaded, we can scale vertically quite far with it.

h2. Nice features:

* Native [backup|https://www.dragonflydb.io/docs/managing-dragonfly/backups] by cron-like schedule
* Native backup storage on S3
* [SSD Data Tiering|https://www.dragonflydb.io/docs/managing-dragonfly/tiering] (alpha and not supported by BITOP and HLL operations)
* [Native|https://www.dragonflydb.io/docs/managing-dragonfly/monitoring] Prometheus monitoring endpoint
* [Search support |https://www.dragonflydb.io/blog/announcing-dragonfly-search]for vectors, close enough to RediSearch module (beta)
* [Forkless bgsave|https://www.dragonflydb.io/blog/balanced-vs-unbalanced] approach, which makes backups more reliable and consistent.

----

Cluster is kinda similar to Redis, but completely lacks any internal remediation, i.e. we need to either build our own control panel to check health of the nodes and promote replicas in case of issues or buy their cloud solution.

{quote}There is one important distinction regarding Dragonfly cluster: Dragonfly only provides a data plane (which is the Dragonfly server), but it does not provide a control plane to manage cluster deployments. Node health monitoring, automatic failovers, slots redistribution are out of scope of Dragonfly backend functionality and are provided as part of Dragonfly Cloud service.{quote}

{quote}Any client-side code that uses Redis Cluster should be able to migrate to Dragonfly Cluster with no changes. Dragonfly Cluster is similar to Redis Cluster in all client facing behavior, but it does not self managed as Redis Cluster in which nodes communicate with each other to discover cluster setup and state.{quote}

{quote}Setting up and managing a Dragonfly Cluster is different from managing a Redis Cluster. Unlike Redis, Dragonfly nodes do not communicate with each other (except for replication). Nodes are unaware of other nodes being unavailable, and cluster configuration is done separately to each node.{quote}

Moreover, their cluster solution also lacks resharding atm.

{quote}Dragonfly does not yet support migration of slots data between nodes. Changing slot allocation will result in data removal.{quote}

----

Look, here’s how I think of the DSA in the context of advertising disclosure. 

There’s a continuum of “advertising’ness” of different stores/restaurants on our platform, with two dimensions:

* nature of the store/restaurant itself: is the existence of the store on the platform an organic consequence of us being a Food Delivery Platform, or not
* nature of the prominence of this store/restaurant: is the prominence of such a store in the UI coming organically from our understanding of how we’re managing the delivery platform based on our understanding of the customer behaviour and marketplace dynamics, or is artificially boosted based on commercial agreements with some third-party. 

For the nature of the store, here are two extremes:

# A regular restaurant that can be organically shown on the platform. Think of McDonalds that has a prominent brand, and whenever a customer would search for McDonald’s, or would search for burger or fast-food places, they would organically see McDonald’s there. This seems to be the least “advertising” type of behaviour. To test for this — if we would de-brand McDonalds on our platform and rename it into “Random affordable burger place with soggy fries“, would we keep it as is on the platform?
# On the other extreme we have stores like “Ice-cream with Magnum“, where the entire existence of this store is coming from an intention to increase the brand presence and sales of Magnum. To test for this: if it’s not branded by Magnum, there’s zero point to running such a store on the platform. 

For the nature of prominence, again two extremes, and I’d say, there are two intermediary states in between:

# A store or a restaurant is simply there, available for customers who want to find it, either by brand name (“McDonald’s“, “Burger King“), or by functional categorisation (“american food“, “fast food“, “burgers“, “something I can get in 20 minutes“ etc.)
# A store or restaurant is getting a prominent position because of how we want to run our marketplace; e. g. there’s a hypothesis that new users are struggling with choosing where to order from for the first several times, so in order to help them with the choice, we’re making specific restaurants/stores more prominent in the app, depending on how well-known brand they have, and we also apply discounts for such restaurants/stores — again, to drive better activation of the customers. The restaurants/stores might be collaborating on this (and might be even investing in the discounts), as such prominence helps them as much as helps us as a platform, but their needs and willingness to collaborate is not the ultimate decision-making driver here, but rather a win-win-win opportunity for us, them and customers.
# A store or restaurant are willing to gain more business on our platform, hence they opt in for investing into campaigns; as long as campaigns make them compelling for customers, we as a platform are willing to give them prominence on the Home Screen, and other high-value parts of the application, which we essentially do. This option differs from the previous one only by the motivational bias: here the restaurant/store owner acts proactively and is primarily optimising for their own interest, and we as a platform facilitate this activity, enhance the effects through visibility, and extract our own interest from this. 
# A store is being artificially put on the Home Screen or other prominent positions because of a very specific commercial agreements with a third party, and irrespective to marketplace or value-add considerations. Realistically, this activity could be even harmful for the marketplace, but we’re taking this trade-off for this or that reason (e. g. we see no way to acquire this store/merchant otherwise, or they are paying us enough to offset the damage).

Now, if my classification is correct (very likely it’s not, as long as *I have zero proficiency in the civil law* — so please do correct it acc to how the regulators are looking at it), it would be great to identify where DSA is applicable, and where not.  

For example, I would imagine us filling in a table like that:

|| ||*organic  natural visibility*||*enhanced visibility  based on marketplace considerations*||*enhanced visibility  based on merchant’s  considerations*||*enhanced visibility based on pure commercial agreements*||
|organic merchant|DSA not applicable, we’ll fight against this in court|DSA might be applicable, but low risk and we will prepare a strategy to object against such classification in court|DSA might be applicable, but low risk as we could always pretend it’s marketplace|DSA obviously applicable, no way out, need to conform|
|artificial merchant|DSA might be applicable, but low risk as it’s hard to distinguish between an artificial merchant and organic merchant|DSA applicable, medium risk
(but close to impossible situation, as artificial merchants do not have any intrinsic value for the marketplace)|DSA obviously applicable, no way out, need to conform|DSA obviously applicable, no way out, need to conform|

Now, given I’m not someone to come up with a legal advice, let’s scratch out what I wrote above, and start from the beginning:

* introduce a relevant classification of activities/solutions we have in therms of advertising’ness of their nature (feel free to build on top of what I produced, but not necessarily)
* formulate a clear advice on where we have bigger/higher risks if we omit DSA disclosures, and what we’re aiming to do with those risks

Hi team, 
Thank you for escalating to Customer Payments team. The customers don't always have a great visibility when the pre-authorization has been returned to them. Returning the pre-authorization is not something Bolt has much control over. 
Depending on the bank the pre-authorization charges can take up to a month to be returned to the customer. 
If the Authorization state is Captured then everything is fine on our side and the customer has to check with their bank. 

Please only escalate the issue to Payment Operations team if

1. The funds have not been returned after 30 days and customer has checked with their bank

2. The state has been stuck in authorization for more than 24 hours. (72h for Micro Mobility) 

3. The state of the authorization is failed or error. 

Please leave a comment on the ticket if you still want it to be escalated to the Customer Payments team. Else the ticket will be closed in 5 days.

*Work Profile: B2C or B2B trip?*

The main consideration would be whether the WP rides would be considered as B2C or B2B transactions - how the ride invoice issued matters and e-invoicing is required for B2B transaction.

* In HU, a transaction qualifies as a B2B transaction when the recipient acts as a taxable person.  Meaning, if a passenger provides both the company name and VAT number in connection with the corporate profile on the WP platform, the ride under WP should be treated as a B2B transaction, e-invoices should be issued via the [+Szamlazz.hu+|http://szamlazz.hu/] platform.  
* However, if the passenger does not provide the VAT number under the WP – which is a required component of the invoice – means that the receipt should be issued in the passenger’s name and the ride would be classified as a B2C transaction.

*What are the implications with the current app setup on Work Profile?*

Currently, it is not mandatory for the passenger to “add company details”.  Or if the passenger chooses to add company details, he only needs to add “company name” and the rest of the information including “VAT ID” and address of the company are optional.  In this regard, 3 scenarios may happen:

# Passenger creates WP *without adding company details* - Ride invoice will be issued by the driver to the passenger directly, it is considered as B2C transaction.
# Passenger creates WP and *adds only company names* - Ride invoice will be issued by the driver to the company, however, as the company details are insufficient to issue a B2B invoice, it is still considered as a B2C transaction. 
# Passenger creates WP and *adds all the company details* (incl. company VAT ID, address, etc. please see below invoice requirements) - Ride invoice (e-invoice) will be issued and fiscalised by the Bolt (on behalf of the driver) to the company via the [+Szamlazz.hu+|http://szamlazz.hu/] platform.  It is considered as a B2B transaction.  

h4. *Invoices requirements - invoice must contain at least the following basic information in HU:*

* The date of issuance of the invoice
* A unique sequential number that identifies the invoice
* The tax number of the supplier who provided the goods or services
* The tax number of the recipient who received the goods or services, for whom the taxpayer is responsible for paying the VAT or for whom a supply of goods was received.
* The full name and address of both the supplier and the customer receiving the goods or services
* A description of the goods or services provided, including the quantity of goods and description of services, as well as the relevant tariff heading or SZJ code, at the discretion of the taxable person issuing the invoice. If applicable, the extent and nature of the services rendered should also be included if it can be expressed in a unit of measurement.
* The date of the invoice, as well as the date of the supply if different from the date of issue of the invoice.
* The taxable amount and unit price of the goods exclusive of VAT.
* If the supply of goods or services is exempt or subject to reverse charge, a reference to the relevant provision of law or any other reference indicating the exemption or reverse charge procedure.
* In the case of intermediaries issuing invoices in triangular transactions subject to the simplification scheme, a legend such as “Triangulation Transaction — Article 141 EC Council Directive 2006/112/EC — Reverse Charge.”
* If a new means of transport is supplied, the invoice must contain data establishing that it is supplied under conditions specified in the VAT Act.
* If the person liable for paying VAT is a financial representative, the invoice must include the name, address, and tax number of the financial representative.
* Other data indicating the use of special regimes, such as self-billing, may also be required.

*Issues?*

* Lack of data quality control and potential non-compliance on e-invoicing
** Under scenarios 2 and 3, how would we validate the company data provided by the passengers is correct?  Especially for scenario 3, e-invoices fiscalised are visible by the companies and the tax authorities and Bolt is obligated to issue the invoices with correct data.  
** Also, is our system ready to identify B2C and B2B WP rides to (i) make sure e-invoices are issued for B2B rides and (ii) make sure the drivers know the difference and they can issue invoices correctly as well?
* Drivers may not be able to identify B2C or B2B WP rides
** As mentioned, in HU, Bolt is allowed to issue B2C invoices on behalf of the drivers.  Drivers is required to issue ride invoices on their own.  Under scenario 2 above, how would the drivers know it is a WP ride and the invoice would be addressed to the company name?  It is a practical question that may need to discuss with the partner.

*Recommendations*

* In view of the above, it is suggested to have WP in HU +only if+ it is a B2C transaction at this moment, meaning the passenger cannot request invoice on company’s name, to avoid any potential non-compliance in invoicing due to incorrect data and system setup.

Dear Ravinder,

Thank you for your data subject rights request, which we received on 31 August 2024.

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, the law requires a data controller such as ourselves to protect the rights of third parties. Furthermore, we must point out that we are not required to disclose documents or otherwise provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

We therefore share copies of the personal data we hold about you to which you are entitled.

Please note that in relation to your payment information, drivers are considered independent contractors providing transportation services via Bolt platform. Due to this, Bolt only stores invoices, pay statement and balance reports of the drivers. This information can be accessed via your Driver Portal available at [https://partners.bolt.eu/login|https://partners.bolt.eu/login]. You can find this information by navigating to the following areas of the Portal:

* Invoices: [https://partners.bolt.eu/invoices|https://partners.bolt.eu/invoices] 
* Pay statements:[ |https://partners.bolt.eu/payouts][https://partners.bolt.eu/payout|https://partners.bolt.eu/payout] 
* Balance reports: [https://partners.bolt.eu/balance-reports|https://partners.bolt.eu/balance-reports]

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

*Your rights* 

In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

If you have any additional questions, please let us know.

Yours sincerely,

*Bolt*

Hi [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd]  and [~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a] , 
+Legal basis indicated by the authority+

* article 6 section 1a - _The controller of the data referred to in paragraph 1a_ *_shall be obliged to make the data available_*_, subject to paragraph 1d,_ +_on the basis of a named authorization of the Commander-in-Chief of the Border Guard, the Commander of the BSWSG, the commander of the Border Guard division or an authorized officer, presented by the officer_+ _together with an official ID card. The fact that this data is made available is subject to protection under the Law of 5 August 2010 on the Protection of Classified Information._
* article 10a section 6 -_The processing of personal data by the Border Police for the purposes referred to in Article 1(1) of the Law of December 14, 2018 on the Protection of Personal Data Processed in Connection with Preventing and Combating Crime shall be carried out on the basis of the Law, European Union law and the provisions of international agreements._

Regulation issued on the basis of paragraph 1d (as mentioned above) states, among others, that:

* The scope of information provided by obligated entities includes:

# _Data about the person, including personal and address data and other identifying data that allow to identify the person, in particular, photographs and image descriptions, features and distinguishing marks, pseudonyms, as well as data specifying family and property relations, education, occupation and sources of income;_
# _description of the event in connection with which the registration of data on the person took place, indicating the date, place and circumstances of its occurrence._

* _The obliged entity may refuse to provide information or limit the scope of information provided if this could result in the disclosure of data of a person who is not an officer of the obliged entity and providing assistance to the obliged entity, or prevent the obliged entity from performing its statutory tasks._

+My opinion:+

* I am of the opinion that *we should provide information requested by the authority*, especially taking into consideration that the proceedings are supervised by the prosecutor and the legal obligation to make the data available as mentioned above. The regulations provides obligation to provide the data. Kindly note that just today we had 2 Police officers at our Warsaw office with a decision of the prosecutor to search our premises for documents requested earlier this year. Bolt refused to provide requested information which could have ended in Police searching our laptops etc.
* However, as underlined above, the request of the authority should be made on the basis of a named authorization. The request was signed by a deputy commander of the border police, therefore in my opinion, *an authorization should be provided prior to making the data available*.
* The response should be provided in writing.

Update:
We are “kind of” taking this as part of the Payment Terms project. I say kind-of because this limit of time for refunds is more a business decision than a legal hard x number of days. There is a x number of days we should use for guidance, as we are, but not taking it as the rule. We will have a global approach of days, which later needs to be validated locally. 

At the end the objective/goal here is for the business to be able to reject old refund requests. The issue is we do not have any time line for anything refunds related. 

Our competitor has a global approach to this. 

The answer to that is of course it depends on the market. However, from a global perspective, it is totally possible to define an internal limit according to the business risk appetite. For this, we should consider:

* What are the regulations around refunds in each market. Meaning:
** Is there an obligation to refund applicable to our services?
** In this same context, what is the limit of time a customer can request a refund according to their consumers law?
* Card Scheme Rules and the rules in regard to chargebacks. A cardholder can request a chargeback within 120/80 days (Visa and MC have different deadlines) after the payment.

The problem seems to be rooted in {{ValidatorInterfaceTraverser.traverseTypeElements}} method.

For regular properties ({{isPropertySignature}}), it calls {{this.interfacesResolver.getCustomTypeManager().getValidators}} to check if there’s a custom validator matching with the property type, while for index signatures ({{isIndexSignatureDeclaration}}) it does not.

The fix seems to be the following:

# Adjust the {{CustomTypeManager.getValidators}} so that it would also accept {{IndexSignatureDeclaration}}.
# Take into account custom type validators in {{isIndexSignatureDeclaration}}.
# [optionally] Refactor the code to reuse the logic of building value validator for {{isIndexSignatureDeclaration}} and {{isPropertySignature}}.

Yes, it is a common practice from the Tax Authority (I think globally) that pending payments that may have existed as a consequence of a service from a specific service provider, is seized and the tax authority request the payment to be made directly to them instead of to the service provider in question.

The logical step would actually be from the tax authority to ask Bolt Operations OÜ to not pay the payout towards the fleet partner and instead pay towards the Tax authority directly. Unfortuantely the tax authority failed to fully understand post payment and bothering our Business Clients. We have tried to inform them so hopefully next time they address directly Bolt Operations OÜ. 

I do not have any information about the nature of the tax. You simply receive an official letter from the tax authority informing you that according to their understanding you own money to X service provider (tax authority automatically receives e-invoices issued by anyone) and they seize the amount therefore you should directly pay towards the authorities.

* Do you also handle this with our verticals using manual adjustment? Under what subtype you use? Do you have an example?

Yes, we can ask for a proof of payment. The amount is whatever that tax authority seize. Tax authority has visibility on the Business invoices and e-invoices are automatically synced with the tax authority in Hungary. 

At the end we can deduct the payment from the fleet account so there is no loss for us. (manual adjustment on the fleet side)

Hi [~accountid:5b8d306bfa38ae2c89608b95] , providing here some Tax input after seeing the ticket, and trying to be as pragmatic as possible:

- Some background: the requirement for merchants to issue fiscal receipts typically stems from a) local tax regulations in the EU member states; fiscalization rules mandate that sellers provide with a fiscal receipt for goods or services sold, as part of the legal obligation to report sales and pay VAT. Additionally, also stems from b) the EU VAT Directive, as set forth by art. 218 (General rule for invoicing), art. 220 (obligation to issue an invoice), art. 219a (content of the invoice), and art. 226 (content of a valid invoice).

- Suggested solution: Providing the customer with a link to the digital receipt issued by IKI. instead of a paper one, the merchant might issue the digital receipt (of course issued from a certified cash register, respecting sequential number, etc.), +provided that the digital format complies with local tax laws+ (to be checked at a Lithuanian Tax law level)

The online link to a digital receipt could ensure that the customer has access to it, while IKI remains responsible for its issuance, and its tax reporting. This link could be included or provided with the Informational Order Summary that we issue for the customer. 
If we want, we could even place a disclaimer specifically for IKI orders, where we request the customer to accept receiving the receipt in digital format only (same applies for credit notes). +All of this would only be applicable if Lithuanian Tax regulations allow for it+.

* _Verification will be and alternative to the already existent method. Though preference goes to this newer method as it is more accurate. Original (physical upload) method will always remain available._

Will any additional data be received from KIWA except for these data points: name, date of birth, adress, company name, adress of company, taxi license number?

* _No additional datapoints except these mentioned above._

Will integrating with KIWA involve sharing our drivers' data back to KIWA or other governmental bodies? If so, what data will be shared, and under what legal framework?

* _No back sharing of any data. We receive a token from the driver which we can use to retrieve data from KIWA (automated through API...)_

Will we store any of the personal data retrieved from KIWA, or will we access it temporarily for verification purposes without retaining it? If we’ll keep it, where will it be stored?

* _Yes we'll save the JSON (name, date of birth, adress, company name, adress of company, taxi license number). As we would also do with the original process._

3. The state of the authorization is failed or error.

Details (aligned with [~accountid:712020:0b1ccfcb-3809-460a-88ab-c96985ba329a]):

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*To summarise the privacy arrangement:*

# both parties will act as separate data controllers - reflecting Bolt`s standard approach. Transfer is two way - both from and to Bolt and Palmpay.
# sections 5.4-5.9 were added to the agreement, which reflect the Bolt`s standard light touch C2C data protection clauses & standard Bolt Business T&C clause 4. They are very general, and on a general level, they clarify:
#* applicable law;
#* procedures for collaboration between the parties, i.e., in case of data breaches;
#* limitation of liability for the parties in relation to personal data - each party is separately liable for its own data processing activities.
# Schedule A clarifies the details of the data transfer - this is the standard schedule of Bolt.
# Schedule B is the Bolts standard Technical and Organisational Security Measures (TOMs) - Palmpay agrees to adhere to them.
# Schedule C - standard Bolt`s EU SCCs reference added, as data will be transferred from Bolt`s EU entity in Estonia to Nigeria.
# Schedule D - custom additional clauses to safeguard the processing of personal data Bolt receives from Palmpay. Specifically:
#* it literally reflects the requirements of the Nigerian law (applicable to controllers) that Bolt undertakes to comply with.
#* clause 3 was added to confirm the limitation on liability for Palmpay, and ensure Palmpay will not be liable for any violation`s of personal data processing from Bolt`s side (duplicating section 5.8 of the Main Agreement).
#* clause 1 clarifies that Bolt is authorised to engage third parties to process personal data (big point of concern and request from Palmpay).
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*What's different from the standard approach:*

* normally we rely on a simple section 4 of the Bolt Business T&C, which clarifies that parties act as independent data controllers, and clarify very basic procedures for collaboration between Bolt and business customers in case of data breaches. In this case, these T&Cs are not applicable.
* in this case, because the customer is substantial, we had to agree to custom terms. These do not contradict the standard approach (where Bolt acts as a data controller), and do not add obligations for Bolt which go beyond what is normally negotiated with business customers.
* main change - custom Schedule D, which clarifies that Bolt will process personal data in compliance with the applicable Nigerian data protection law.
{panel}

But also possible if Operations config is adjusted with new accounts and retry is done resulting in new accounts/entry types only on one side (given we don’t have versioning yet). Or when posting key is reused for both parts of the current transaction chain. Its just a case that came up during testing, but not live (afaik).

Hard to say what the exact reasons are atm given live integration is disabled, but cleaning up errors and adding better safety to racing queries should improve the situation significantly (if not eliminate alltogether).

{quote}lock the key for a posting with Redis on Journal side → How much will it affect performance?{quote}

It should in our current case even improve performance as we are not processing the same request n times in parallel, only one at a time making other parallel retries idempotent (given payments at some point sent us duplicate event like 2-4x in parallel for some reason).

It provides us better safety against racing queries, but does introduce a new point of failure - the latter point we wanted to explore in this task: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/CBFP-575|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/CBFP-575|smart-link]

As a summary, I do not see blockers to start deployment of this new feature in PT. However, it is recommended to ensure that the privacy team is aware to allow transparency in the PT privacy notice to drivers.

Please see below my thoughts:

* *T&Cs changes not required*: The PT T&Cs for TVDE operators do not currently need to be changed, as they do not include any information about the dispatching logic. 
* *Local ride-hailing regulation:* The local regulation does not include requirements on dispatching logic.
* *Reclassification considerations:* linking the DQO to the Blast Dispatch won’t increase the risk level of the market as turning on the DQO already increased the risk significantly as we noted in [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-30071|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-30071|smart-link]In PT the risk was accepted by all stakeholders, as these are measures aim to counterbalance the negative impacts for the business of removing the automatic and statistical blocking with the idea to influence drivers’ behaviour from a positive perspective. The reclassification risk is however still high since these features could be seen as a restriction of drivers' autonomy regarding the possibility of accepting or refusing tasks. This is a business decision.
* *Dispatching logic subject to disclosure*: The dispatching logic is subject to disclosure in the event of legal proceedings or a request from the PT transport regulator (the AMT) or labour regulator (the ACT). The dispatching logic must also be reflected in the privacy notice if personal data of the drivers are processed for this purpose (included in the draft of the updated privacy notice). Thanks for reaching out.
That's not an actual increase. Failed payments are not directly connected to fraud. Good users have failed payments all the time due to lack of funds, temporary problems on the issuer side and so on. 
Failed payments have great recovery. Good users recover failed payments with a ratio even above 80% in some markets. With that in mind, it's absolutely normal that the fresher the data, the worse failed payments will be - even though the name is final failed payment, they're not really final. they're more like actual failed payments. 
For final numbers, need to give it like 2-3 months, and for failed pays older than, recovery likely won't happen anymore. We should expect to recover to around ~0.25.
Best,
Karl

Thank you for escalating to Customer Payments team. The customers don't always have a great visibility when the pre-authorization has been returned to them. Returning the pre-authorization is not something Bolt has much control over. 
Depending on the bank the pre-authorization charges can take up to a month to be returned to the customer. 
If the Authorization state is Captured then everything is fine on our side and the customer has to check with their bank. 

Please only escalate the issue to Payment Operations team if

1. The funds have not been returned after 30 days and customer has checked with their bank

2. The state has been stuck in authorization for more than 24 hours. (72h for Micro Mobility) 

3. The state of the authorization is failed or error. 

Please leave a comment on the ticket if you still want it to be escalated to the Customer Payments team. Else the ticket will be closed in 5 days.

+*CONTEXT*+

“_There is a driver in Poland that has a YT channel (_ [https://www.youtube.com/@Arturas_Laucius|https://www.youtube.com/@Arturas_Laucius|smart-link]  _). He records his passengers without blurring their faces and uploads the videos online. There is a video where he is fighting with the riders_ [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FCOJbSA5MI8&t=15s|https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FCOJbSA5MI8&t=15s|smart-link] 
_He claims to be a driver on different platforms so this poses a PR risk to us. Can we block him?_
_Also - there are more and more drivers who use private dashcams and record riders. Can we do something about this issue? Should the drivers be obliged to register the cameras in our app? Should we send the riders notifications that there is a possibility that they will be recorded? Or maybe the drivers should be obliged to use stickers that inform about the dashcam?_”

----

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
+*SUMMARY OF THOUGHTS*+

* The issue of whether to block the driver is not necessarily for privacy to lead on.
* We should check with the legal team whether requiring drivers to register their own cameras on the Bolt app would trigger any reclass risk. It would be better to encourage drivers to register on a voluntary basis, however this may not resolve the present issue.
* In terms of notifying the rider of a dashcam, it would probably be more effective to notify the rider in-app than to ask the driver to install a sticker in their car. However, we would need to carefully tailor the language to mitigate any controllership issues. It may be worth checking what Uber previously did on this.
* Ultimately, the more we do about the ‘issue’ of drivers installing dashcams, the more we run the risk of privacy / reclass issues. [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd] - given your previous experience with this issue, {color:#4c9aff}*do you have any additional thoughts*{color}?
{panel}

----

+*MORE DETAILED THOUGHTS*+

*(1) General*

* Poland is a sensitive market in terms of CCTV / privacy. ATR launch in Poland gathered over 300 media clippings and caused some controversy in our dialogue with Ministry of Digital Affairs
* Generally (as in Poland), Bolt does not mandate the installation of dashcams (this amounts to providing work equipment, and so has reclass risk). In [LSS-35669|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-35669], it was agreed that Bolt could negotiate a deal with dashcam providers, but not provide them to fleets (i.e., the fleet should be purchasing them).
* Bolt should not have access to CCTV footage, as this would raise a number of privacy concerns. Equally, Bolt should avoid gathering recordings.
* Nevertheless, riders should be aware that they are being recorded. This would primarily be the responsibility of the controller of the data to arrange.

*(2) Can we block him?*

This is not a privacy issue _per se_. Ultimately, if the driver has violated Bolt’s Terms, then we would have grounds for blocking. Otherwise, this would pose a risk.

*(3) Should the drivers be obliged to register the cameras in our app?*

We do not generally mandate drivers to install dashcams, due to reclass risk. 
If a driver chooses to install a camera in their car, and we require the driver to register the camera in our app, this is not quite the same as requiring the driver to install the camera in the first place. However, it would be worth checking with the wider team whether this would similarly trigger reclass risk.
It is worth noting that Uber previously took this approach in 2023 (see [here|https://www.uber.com/en-GB/blog/london/register-your-dashcam/#:~:text=Uber%20will%20notify%20riders%20if,trip%20with%20a%20different%20driver.]), but made it _voluntary_ for drivers to register the dashcam. This could be a way of mitigating reclass risk. However, for drivers like the one raised in this ticket, they may not do so.
In either case, provided that the driver chooses whether to install the camera and Bolt does not have access to the data, this proposed option does not _directly_ raise privacy concerns. We would just be collecting additional personal data about the driver (i.e., whether they have a dashcam or not).

*(4) Should we send the riders notifications that there is a possibility that they will be recorded? Or maybe the drivers should be obliged to use stickers that inform about the dashcam?*

The relevant controller of the recording would be the driver here, not Bolt. As such, it is primarily the responsibility of the driver to inform the rider that the rider is being recorded, and we should not be sending the rider any sort of full disclaimer / transparency wording (as this creates the risk of presenting Bolt as the controller). This is particularly important due to the sensitivity of the CCTV issue in Poland.
We _could_ encourage drivers to include stickers in their cars, but we could not make this mandatory as otherwise we would be creeping back towards the reclass / privacy issues raised above. It would be totally up to the driver whether to include the sticker, and so this would probably not solve the issue that we have been tagged in for this ticket.
We _could_ notify riders in-app that there is the possibility that the ride would be recorded. This was the approach taken by Uber in 2023 (see [here|https://www.uber.com/en-GB/blog/london/register-your-dashcam/#:~:text=Uber%20will%20notify%20riders%20if,trip%20with%20a%20different%20driver.]). However:
* If this is being sent out to all riders (on the basis that we do not currently know which drivers have installed dashcams) then this may cause concerns / a wave of DSARs from riders for dashcam footage - we could deal with these, but it would create bandwidth issues.
* If this was being sent out only to riders where the driver had installed a dashcam, then we would need to collect additional driver data per issue (3) above (as Uber did). First, we need to check with the legal team from a reclass perspective.
In either case, the notification language would need to explicitly state that it is the driver that chooses to install the camera etc. It may be worth seeing if Uber still does this, and if so what language they use.

Currently, we are of the opinion that drivers = independent controllers and therefore we do not control the use of their cameras. This is in line with GDPR, where we, as an independent controller, don’t give instructions to another independent controller.

*Some Beehive articles on this - responses to riders and drivers/fleets on their use of cameras:*

* [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/33697?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/33697?country=global&language=en]
* [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/23948?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/23948?country=global&language=en]



Therefore, we can’t push drivers to have any signs, we can only advise them. 

Antoni Wende and Sarra Eddahiri will be working on a global project regarding dashcams/CCTV in cars (see ticket [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-35669|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-35669|smart-link] ), but the project has been postponed. This project will cover the information obligations, as well as in-app notifications. Me/Alon will be working on this project together with Product Legal and GFT, but it didn’t seem to cut the MVRA for Q4. 

From privacy POV, pushing any obligations to drivers will pose us reclass and privacy risks. The camera use in cars was already raised by AKI during a meeting with us, following an escalation from the Spanish DPA. We stuck to our position - we are independent, we don’t have control over drivers so we can’t make them do this.

What we can do is remind the drivers that they need to comply with applicable laws.

*Blocking*
{panel}

I suggest pushing back - analyzing whether there was a breach of T&Cs and whether we can take action against drivers for it does not fall under our competencies, it’s for GFT to assess.

De acordo com a legislação em vigor, a ” prestação do serviço de TVDE pode ser remunerada pela aplicação de uma ou mais tarifas à distância percorrida e/ou ao tempo despendido no transporte, ou pela aplicação de um preço fixo determinado antes da contratação do serviço.” 

Neste sentido, os termos e condições da Bolt aceites pelo operador TVDE ao serviço do qual o motorista presta serviços estabelecem:

“5.2. A proposta de preço fixo pré-determinado é comunicada ao Utilizador e ao Operador TVDE (eventualmente, através do Motorista que atue em sua representação) através da App Bolt antes da prestação do Serviço de Transporte. “

Melhores cumprimentos,

Confidential Information includes information that is (a) disclosed by Discloser in writing shall be marked at the time of disclosure to indicate it is confidential; (b) disclosed by Discloser in any other manner and is indicated at the time of disclosure to be confidential; (c) disclosed by Discloser in the form of tangible materials transmitted to Recipient with a writing designating materials as confidential; (d) disclosed to or obtained by Recipient through a tour of Discloser's facilities; or (e) reasonably understood by Recipient to be confidential. [[3M1]|]3M would like to retain the original language here. 3M believes that marking requirement is an integral part of a CDA. *Initial thoughts based on ticket and RFC*: We should notify users that responses are aided by translation tools and limit the use of machine translation to low risk CS interactions. 

*Limit DeepL use to low-risk, routine CS interactions and notify users of machine translation tool use.* High-risk cases (e.g., safety-related tickets, high-value claims, privacy complaints or worker classification issues) should be escalated to native-speaking staff (e.g. local ops) and/or legal in line with existing escalation processes. I’d also recommend notifying users when responses are aided by translation tools to maintain transparency and meet local consumer law obligations in all markets; unless doing so significantly impacts user experience.

h3. Specific Challenges and Mitigations:

# *Complex Legal Terminology:*
*Problem:* Different EU countries, and countries outside the EU where Bolt operates, have distinct legal terminologies and frameworks. A term used in one country may not have a direct legal counterpart in another, which could create discrepancies communications with users. DeepL may misinterpret terms that have legal consequences, leading to inaccuracies or unintended assumption of liability by Bolt.
*Mitigation:* Use DeepL for routine inquiries only. High-risk interactions should be escalated to native speakers in local ops or legal. Notifying users that translation tools are used may also mitigate the risk in the event mistakes are made in early CS interactions.
# *Cultural Differences:*
*Problem:* Machine translations can miss cultural nuances, leading to potential miscommunication.
*Mitigation:* Routine inquiries can be handled by DeepL; sensitive cases must be escalated. Inform users about translation tool usage unless it significantly detracts from the UX. As suggested in the RFC, thoroughly testing the language models prior to implementation and periodic checks by native speakers will also help mitigate this risk.
# *Confidentiality, User Privacy and Ethical Considerations:*
*Problem:* Machine translation could expose sensitive user data.
*Mitigation:* High-risk cases involving sensitive data should use manual translation and sensitive/identifiable user data should not be entered into translation tools where possible. Ensure DeepL’s strictest privacy settings are enabled for routine cases. Suggest privacy review (cc: [~accountid:712020:0c8dd65b-46d5-4dc0-b5bd-76209c1e8048]) to ensure DPAs and relevant EU/National privacy risks adequately mapped and mitigated.

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.

Hi [~accountid:63a562e8082abdd71bb435b6] / [~accountid:712020:0f7a089b-3b06-423b-844c-6e5ac370aa1e] 

I see there are a few commercial terms pending - please advise whether the wording needs to be amended regarding the following points:
1.  *Clause 2 - Auto-renewal* - _the agreement autimatically renews for successive one year terms unless either Party provides a written notice of non-renewal at least 60 days prior to then-current term_. It is advisable for Bolt to negotiate for a shorter notice period for non-renewal. A 60-day notice period may be too long and could potentially lock Bolt into another year of service that it may not want or need. Proposed alternatives: (1) Recommended notice period 30 days before the expiry of the term OR we could replace it with a right to terminate for convenience at any time giving X days prior notice.
2. *Clause 7 - Warranties:* _The Parties acknowledge that MapUp's SDK products are provided "AS IS," without any warranty of any kind, express or implied_. This *"AS IS"* clause could potentially expose Bolt to risk if the SDK products have defects or do not perform as expected. It is suggested to negotiate for at least a limited warranty that the SDK products will function as described in the technical documentation provided by MapUp.

Hello,

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.

Hello,

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.
