[2024-09 Prague DV360 Android launch|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MP/pages/5411504148/2024-09+Prague+DV360+Android+launch] - *No incrementality*. Launch of the new channel and investment 881 EUR daily did not show any statistically significant increase in signups.
[2024-09 Kyiv Google iOS launch|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MP/pages/5411110974/2024-09+Kyiv+Google+iOS+launch] - *Inconclusive.* Launch of the new IOS channel resulted in the statistically significant drop in signups. There was a clear breakup of the android/iOS relationship after the test launch. Moreover there was an unexpected spike in Android installs.

That spike was caused by the fraudulent signups. After taking a closer look it turned out that *56%* of the signups 25-26 Sep didn’t have their phone verified. But even by eliminating them from analysis the experiment shows statistically significant drop.
[2024-09 Valletta Google Android drop|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MP/pages/5413437911/2024-09+Valletta+Google+Android+drop] - *Incrementality.* (finally!) We observe a statistically significant drop in signups when the budget was reduced by 300 EUR. The results might be affected by a tourist outflow, but since we did a test on Android that is less probable.

[Technical note] What I personally expected in this experiment is “inconclusive”. As the summer period ends we observe a huge decline in iOS installs (tourists). Our model should have predicted then a similar decline in Android because both platforms are “tied” by counterfactual assumption. Assuming the fluctuations of Android tourist signups are less affected by seasonality we should have got inconsistent results - we observe more android signups than model predicts and conclude the statistically significant uplift. Given that we have dropped the budgets that should have given “inconclusive”. However that didn’t happen, which most likely means we have a very good signal of marketing influence and very high ROI. The results suggest obviously highly invest in that market.
[2024-09 Bratislava Google (Youtube) iOS launch|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MP/pages/5419696424/2024-09+Bratislava+Google+Youtube+iOS+launch] - *No incrementality.* Launch of Youtube campaign didn’t result in the statistically significant increase in signups. Moreover, we were close to conclude the signup drop which is a clear sign of android-iOS relationship breakage during the test period.
[2024-09 Bucharest DV360 iOS launch|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MP/pages/5419729292/2024-09+Bucharest+DV360+iOS+launch] - *Incrementality* (finally!). Launch of the new DV360 channel shows the statistically significant increase in signups.

[2024-09 Stockholm DV360 iOS launch|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MP/pages/5419401808/2024-09+Stockholm+DV360+iOS+launch] - *No incrementality.* Increase in spend from 0 to 970 daily didn’t lead to any statistically significant increase in signups.
[2024-09 Zagreb Meta Android increse|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MP/pages/5419172248/2023-09+Zagreb+Meta+Android+increase] - *Incrementality.* Increase from 153 to 379 resulted in 16 more signups daily.

** INTERNAL UPDATE **

+*Background*+

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*In short:*

* User A used to own Account 1, but does not have access anymore since they changed their phone number from the Old Phone Number to the New Phone Number. User A’s Payment Method was left on Account 1. User A seems to be unaware that Account 1 is still active.
* User B now has access to Account 1 as a result of getting the recycled Old Phone Number. User B is using User A’s Payment Method to conduct trips. As the Payment Method is connected to User A’s bank account, User A is being notified of these charges.
* This would count as a personal data breach, as User B has unauthorised access to Account 1. Furthermore, if User B is continuing to use the Payment Method, then User A is continuing to suffer financial detriment, which we need to fix ASAP.
* The main outstanding fact-finding issue is that it looks like Account 1 and Account 2 both had the Old Phone Number listed for the period between 29 May and 10 June - I thought a phone number could not be used on two rider accounts simultaneously?
{panel}

*UPDATED SUMMARY OF BACKGROUND*

* [This Bolt account|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/105184270/overview?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] (“*Account 1*”) was created in January 2022, and is still active.
** On 29 May 2024, the details of Account 1 were changed, including name (to Lukauskas Raimondas), email ([raimondas@neaustima.lt|mailto:raimondas@neaustima.lt] - “*Email Address 1*”), phone number (to +37068733606 - the “*Old Phone Number*”) and birthday (to 1961-01-23).
** Presumably, at this point, Account 1 was under the control of Raimondas Lukauskss, the rider who has raised this issue to us (“*User A*”) - This is because in User A’s [request|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/420399787] submitted to us on 8 August 2024, User A stated that they have previously owned the Old Phone Number.
** There is currently only one active payment method on Account 1 (a card ending in 7283), which was added on 27 November 2023 (the “*Payment Method*”).
* It seems that User A also previously had another Bolt account ([here|https://admin.bolt.eu/user/Users/user/219157835] - “*Account 2*”).
** On 10 June 2024, the email address on Account 2 was changed to [raimondss.lukauskas@splius.lt|mailto:raimondss.lukauskas@splius.lt] (“*Email Address 2*”), and the phone number was changed from the Old Phone Number to +37066795522 (the “*New Phone Number*”).
* On 30 July 2024, User A noticed two charges for trips they claim they did not take.
** User A claims that based on discussions with Bolt CS, this was because the Old Phone Number has been recycled and is being used by another user (“*User B*”), whose specific identity we do not know. Presumably, User B gained access to Account 1 on 19 June 2024 (when the login from a new device was registered on Account 1).
** These two charges come from Account 1, as they match trips taken in Account 1’s order history. These trips were all paid for using the Payment Method.
** User A is receiving these receipts due to their bank account being linked to the Payment Method (i.e., they appear to be bank statements retrieved from the user’s online banking).
* As a result of the unrecognised charges, User A deleted Account 2 on 30 July 2024, and created a new Bolt account ([here|https://admin.bolt.eu/user/Users/user/226045933] - “*Account 3*”), using the New Phone Number.
* On 23 August 2024, User A noticed another charge for a trip they did not take.
** User A claims that based on discussions with Bolt CS, this was again due to a recycled phone number issue. Again, this charge matches a trip taken on Account 1, and was paid for using the Payment Method.
* As a result of the additional unrecognised receipt, User A deleted Account 3 on 25 August 2024.
* On 19 September 2024, User created another Bolt account ([here|https://admin.bolt.eu/user/Users/user/233146806] - “*Account 4*”) using the New Phone Number and Email Address 2. Account 4 does not have a connected payment method. This suggests User A wants to continue using Bolt.

+*Next Steps*+

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*In short:*

* Report to DPO as a personal data breach (x1 - User B access to User A’s Account 1).
* I need to also align with the wider Privacy Team before taking the below steps, to check whether this approach is viable.
* We should archive Account 1, and inform User B that they need to create a new Bolt account.
* We should ask User A to freeze / block their Payment Method for good measure.


{panel}

*Further details*

* See [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-36090|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-36090|smart-link] for similar logic applied on a similar ticket.
* *Step 1*: We should temporarily block Account 1.
* *Step 2*: Get User A to contact their bank and ask them to contact their bank to freeze / block the Payment Method. This would mean that User B can no longer cause financial detriment to User A.
* *Step 3*: Inform User B of the situation (re why Account 1 blocked) and ask them to create a new Bolt account. This would mean that User B no longer has access to any of User A’s personal data from Account 1. To smooth the situation, we could consider providing User B with the order history of the trips they took, to satisfy possible DSAR issues in future.

* (1) Determine the usual means of responding to the Border Guard (I note that you have seen similar requests from the Border Guard before).
* (2) Ask for the following from the Border Guard (in writing, using the means of communication identified above) before providing the requested data:
** (a) Named authorisation to request the information from the Commander-in-Chief of the Border Guard, the Commander of the BSWSG, the commander of the Border Guard division or an authorised officer.
** (b) Confirmation that what the Border Guard are requesting is a digital copy of the passport.
** (c) Further details on why the Border Guard need this information (i.e., anything they can tell us about the allegation / crime / proceedings).
* (3) Once the Border Guard provides the above (particularly (a) and (b). Point (c) we can ultimately live without if pressed), then source and provide a digital copy of the passport as requested.

If helpful, I include some more details on the reasoning below. Let me know if you have any questions on this.

*Further details*

+Means of responding+
Per advice from local counsel, our response should be in writing.
As such, please check how we ordinarily respond to request from the Border Guard, and if that is through a written channel, then please submit our follow-up requests via that channel, quoting any appropriate reference number(s) so that the Border Guard know what we are referring to.
+Named authorisation+
The Border Guard has indicated that their legal basis for requesting this information is Article 6 Section 1(a), which states “_The controller of the data referred to in paragraph 1a shall be obliged to make the data available, subject to paragraph 1d,_ +_on the basis of a named authorization of the Commander-in-Chief of the Border Guard, the Commander of the BSWSG, the commander of the Border Guard division or an authorized officer, presented by the officer_+ _together with an official ID card.”_
The request we have received from the Border Guard is signed by a deputy commander of the border police. As such, we do not appear to have a named authorisation as specified above. Per advice from local counsel, we need to obtain this before we are obliged to provide the information.
+Providing the digital copy of the passport+
From a Privacy perspective, we should be providing the minimal amount of data possible. Fortunately, the Border Guard are only requesting one document relating to one individual - if we are able to confirm this, then this seems proportionate from our side, all things considered.
Per advice from local counsel, we should provide this information to the Border Guard, especially taking into consideration that the proceedings are supervised by the prosecutor and Bolt is under a legal obligation to make this information available upon receipt of a proper request.

analysis was done by looking at data from July/2024. 

I’ve pulled every in-app order that didn’t have preauth. main metric will be from the columns:

* *max_risk_cost*: the assumption is that if an order had an initial failed payment, the user could run into the same error in the preauth that could cause the order not to be created. _max_risk_cost_ tracks the worst possible scenario where every single order that matches this criteria ends up not being created. loss to us is the order GMV vs Rides 8% profitability. 
* *min_savings_same_price*: this column represents our main saving. if the order’s final price remains equal to or smaller than the amount we have authorized and is currently uncovered, then the payment won’t fail anymore. 

*max_risk_cost* isn’t realistic. users should be able to change payment methods or top-up their cards to still create orders. 

on the other end, *min_savings_same_price* is a guaranteed win.

therefore, if (*min_savings_same_price* - *max_risk_cost*) is positive, the outcome should be positive for Bolt. 

the tab *_simplified numbers on the country level_* on the following sheet has country numbers: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/18v_OnyknnNbaIIj3dDIbn18zSd5F8h5328-QX5bvICk/edit?gid=0#gid=0|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/18v_OnyknnNbaIIj3dDIbn18zSd5F8h5328-QX5bvICk/edit?gid=0#gid=0|smart-link] 

for some countries, if we start doing preauth for literally every single in-app order, the outcome should be positive. TH for example, has a *max_risk_cost* of 5.4k euros and *min_savings_same_price* of 10.1k euros. we would reduce 10.1k euros in failed payments risking at max 5.4k euros of net good GMV.

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount.

After talking more with the agent who initially raised this topic, the blatant answer to your last question would be not wanting to make the calls.

Subjectively, at the risk of sounding dismissive, a fair amount of cases involving these ECs (Food Poisoning/Foreign object in food/Spoiled item) are connected to eater-fraud: repetitive, shallow reports that tick all the boxes for a compensation.
The agents feel that ‘their time would be better utilised on the next ticket instead of calling to talk about a piece of rock in a salad, where we already have a picture of it.’ This would also apply to Bolt Market deliveries, where, confidently, a moldy fruit found after unpacking the delivery bag is the number one cause for a safety ticket.

I agree that food poisoning out of these three is by far the most sensitive and important topic. I feel that the agents might understand calling to be mostly an investigation tool and less of a way to show we care and let our users feel heard. Perceiving any truth to a case being fraudulent should only be a by-product of a call.

I would still like to challenge calling in cases of the other two ECs. Unless the user bit down on the rock they found in their salad, I feel making a call would be a misplacement of resources.

{{Case 4 - Weekend fraud}}

We face more fraud trips on the weekend due to the fraudsters assuming they will go undetected as we are not actively working as well as them knowing our ‘defences’ are often run once a day. Therefore, we have faced quite many scenarios where in the morning of Monday when payouts are paid out early hours, automatic defences (refunds/blocks) have yet to kick in but the money is already leaving and Bolt is left with debted drivers never intending to pay it back. 

While we can’t assume all volume that is highlighted is actual fraud, we can see there is definitely a connection between weekend and hightened payment problems.

We are looking at cases where overall volumes don’t contain high problems (overall sums <0.5 problematic) but the weekend has higher problematic ratios (weekend sums >0.7 problematic.

!Screenshot 2024-10-03 at 11.54.36.png|width=885,height=676,alt="Screenshot 2024-10-03 at 11.54.36.png"!

UK pops up significantly and this can be due to multiple reasons: 1) it is an expensive market 2) historically (annually) we have not had the means to target fraud so the loss is incurring 3) the nature of the market - there are a lot of weekend drivers. 

Without including UK as the outlier, there is an opportunity impact of {color:#bf2600}*82K eur annually and 6.2K eur monthly.* {color}Including UK (keeping in mind that there further breakdowns would be needed to target weekend fraud), the opportunity raises to *185k eur annually and 15K eur monthly* with just UK making 102K eur annual and 8.5K eur monthly volumes. 

*Payouts containing bad weekend volumes*

{noformat}----------------- /////// AGGREGATES /////// ---------------
SELECT 
x.country,
	sum(x.sum_total_problem_orders) AS sum_problems_eur,
	sum(x.weekend_sum_total_problem_orders_from_total) AS sum_problems_weekend,
	approx_distinct(x.payout_id,0.0041) AS count_payouts,
	approx_distinct(x.driver,0.0041) AS count_drivers
from(
WITH stats AS(
		--
		SELECT
		co.driver_courier_id AS driver_id,
		date_trunc('week',co.created) AS week_stats,
			--(CASE WHEN co.created BETWEEN date('2023-10-29') AND date('2024-03-30') THEN co.created  + INTERVAL '3' HOUR ELSE co.created  + INTERVAL '4' HOUR END)) AS week_stats,
		co.country_code AS country_code,
		approx_distinct(co.order_id,0.0041) AS all_orders,
		round(COALESCE (sum(co.partner_price_eur),0),0) AS all_orders_sum,
		--
		--- INAPP VOLUME -----
		--
		round(COALESCE(sum(CASE WHEN co.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN co.partner_price_eur ELSE 0 END),0),0) AS sum_inapp,
		approx_distinct(CASE WHEN co.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN co.order_id ELSE 0 END,0.0041) AS count_inapp,
		-- FRAUD PROBLEM TOTAL 
		--
		round(COALESCE(sum(CASE WHEN co.driver_courier_fraud_label = TRUE OR co.is_chargeback = TRUE or co.propagated_chargeback = TRUE OR co.is_final_failed_payment = TRUE OR co.is_payment_problem = TRUE THEN co.partner_price_eur ELSE 0 END),0),0) AS sum_total_problem_orders,
		approx_distinct(CASE WHEN co.driver_courier_fraud_label = TRUE OR co.is_chargeback = TRUE or co.propagated_chargeback = TRUE OR co.is_final_failed_payment = TRUE OR co.is_payment_problem = TRUE THEN co.order_id END,0.0041) AS count_total_problem_orders,
		round(COALESCE(sum(CASE WHEN co.driver_courier_fraud_label = TRUE OR co.is_chargeback = TRUE or co.propagated_chargeback = TRUE OR co.is_final_failed_payment = TRUE OR co.is_payment_problem = TRUE THEN co.partner_price_eur ELSE 0 END)/NULLIF(sum(co.partner_price_eur),0),0),1) AS ratio_total_problem_sum,
		--
		--WEEKEND FRAUD FROM TOTAL ------
		round(COALESCE(sum(CASE WHEN day_of_week(co.created) IN (6,7) AND (co.driver_courier_fraud_label = TRUE OR co.is_chargeback = TRUE or co.propagated_chargeback = TRUE OR co.is_final_failed_payment = TRUE OR co.is_payment_problem = TRUE) THEN co.partner_price_eur ELSE 0 END),0),0) AS weekend_sum_total_problem_orders_from_total,
		approx_distinct(CASE WHEN day_of_week(co.created) IN (6,7) AND (co.driver_courier_fraud_label = TRUE OR co.is_chargeback = TRUE or co.propagated_chargeback = TRUE OR co.is_final_failed_payment = TRUE OR co.is_payment_problem = TRUE) THEN co.order_id END,0.0041) AS weekend_count_total_problem_orders_from_total,
		round(COALESCE(sum(CASE WHEN day_of_week(co.created) IN (6,7) AND (co.driver_courier_fraud_label = TRUE OR co.is_chargeback = TRUE or co.propagated_chargeback = TRUE OR co.is_final_failed_payment = TRUE OR co.is_payment_problem = TRUE) THEN co.partner_price_eur ELSE 0 END)/NULLIF(sum(co.partner_price_eur),0),0),1) AS weekend_ratio_total_problem_sum_from_total,
		--
		--WEEKEND FRAUD EXCLUSIVELY------
		round(COALESCE(sum(CASE WHEN day_of_week(co.created) IN (6,7) AND (co.driver_courier_fraud_label = TRUE OR co.is_chargeback = TRUE or co.propagated_chargeback = TRUE OR co.is_final_failed_payment = TRUE OR co.is_payment_problem = TRUE) THEN co.partner_price_eur ELSE 0 END)/NULLIF(sum(CASE WHEN day_of_week(co.created) IN (6,7) THEN co.partner_price_eur ELSE 0 END),0),0),1) AS weekend_ratio_total_problem_sum_from_weekend
		--
		FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders AS co
		WHERE co.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -14, CURRENT_DATE) AS date)
		AND co.order_type ='rides' AND co.order_state = 'finished'
		AND co.payment_method_group = 'in-app'
		GROUP BY 1,2,3
		)
		SELECT
		DISTINCT pp.id AS payout_id,
				date_trunc('week',pp.created) AS created_week_payout,
				date_diff('day',s.week_stats,date_trunc('week',pp.created)) AS diff_created_sanity_check,
				s.week_stats AS created_week_orders,
				ca.country,
				pp.client_id,
				pc.external_id AS driver,
				s.*,
				pp.created_date AS creation_date_payout,
				pp.amount AS amount,
				pp.currency AS currency,
				round(pp.amount /r.rate,0) AS payout_eur,
				pp."method" AS method,
				pp.state AS state,
				pp."type" AS TYPE
					FROM  glue.ng_payout.invoicing_payment_payout AS pp
					LEFT JOIN glue.ng_payout.invoicing_payment_client AS pc ON pp.client_id = pc.id
					LEFT JOIN glue.ng_payout.invoicing_payment_client_account AS ca ON pp.client_id = ca.client_id 
					LEFT JOIN glue.ng_public.vw_currency_exchange_rates r ON r.currency = pp.currency AND date(r.valid_on) = date(pp.created)
					LEFT JOIN stats AS s ON pc.external_id = s.driver_id 
							AND s.week_stats = date_trunc('week',pp.created) - INTERVAL '7' DAY
		WHERE 
		pp."method" = 'regular'
		AND 
		pp."type" = 'ride_hailing_driver'
		AND
		pp.state = 'finished'
		--AND 
		--s.driver_id IS NOT NULL
		--AND
		--pc.external_id = 2607478
		--AND ca.country = 'be'
		--AND s.ratio_total_problem_sum > 0.5
		--AND CASE WHEN 
		--AND CASE WHEN ca.country = 'gb' THEN (s.weekend_sum_total_problem_orders_from_total >= 150 OR s.weekend_count_total_problem_orders_from_total > 1) END
		AND pp.created  >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -12, CURRENT_DATE) AS date)
		--AND date_diff('day',s.week_stats,date_trunc('week',pp.created)) > 7
		--AND round(pp.amount /r.rate,0) > 200
		ORDER BY 2 DESC 
)AS x
WHERE 
x.weekend_ratio_total_problem_sum_from_total < 0.5
AND 
x.weekend_ratio_total_problem_sum_from_weekend > 0.7
--AND
--x.country <> 'gb'
--CASE WHEN x.country = 'gb' OR  x.country = 'fr' THEN (x.weekend_sum_total_problem_orders_from_total >= 150 OR x.weekend_count_total_problem_orders_from_total > 1) ELSE (x.weekend_sum_total_problem_orders_from_total >= 25 OR x.weekend_count_total_problem_orders_from_total > 1) END
GROUP BY 1{noformat}

After a quick look, here are some ideas.

I think the best way to generate the report is to add code to the generator, but potentially before it’s printing the configless files. The reason is that there is sharding, which is much easier to detect before it’s expanded, and that there are also naming exceptions which don’t really matter for the statistics. There is {{SnsSqsProvisioningConfigLoader}} class which transforms raw bootstrap results (parsed publishers + subscribers) into the data printed to files later. Generation happens per-environment, but the biggest difference is between local and non-local envs, so the stats can be gathered for live and they should be pretty much identical for prelive.

As for sharding, we have sharding for SQS subscribers, as in queue+subscription generated per shard, and subscription can be automatically filtered by {{shard_id}}. There are also a couple of cases of sharded SQS *provider* (as in SQS only), for example: [https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/940b29c1ce53fc7fcadee4d9ce0f91254ce2b2cc/src/platform/geo/tracking/main/tracking_rental/BootstrapCron.ts#L34-L35|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/940b29c1ce53fc7fcadee4d9ce0f91254ce2b2cc/src/platform/geo/tracking/main/tracking_rental/BootstrapCron.ts#L34-L35] But from what I can see, we don’t have sharded SNS, and even if the service itself is sharded, then all shards publish to the same SNS resource, which can then be consumed both by sharded and non-sharded services.

So for the sake of statistics, these would probably be the most interesting setups to differentiate:

# SNS + SQS – all with non-empty subscriber names
## Implementation hints
### Each queue corresponds 1-to-1 to a subscription, in code both are generated from the same list of {{bootstrapResult.mq_subscribers}}, and they both are owned by the same service/owner. The only difference is that subscription contains the filters.
### Make sure to filter out data by {{SubscriberType.CLASSIC}}, {{MqPublisherMatchType.AWS_(SNS|SQS)}}, {{PublisherType.(regular|db)}} (yeah, it’s a mess 😕)
## By number of subscribers
### With 0 subscribers – should be a weird case where SNS is consumed externally or the consumer hasn’t been released yet
### With 1 subscriber
#### Subscriber is unsharded – potentially waisting costs instead of just using SQS directly (this is one of the main goals of the report from what I understand)
#### Subscriber is sharded – we have >1 shard everywhere from what I know, so it’s an ok setup
### With >1 subscribers (could be mix of sharded and unsharded) – ok setup
## By publisher type
### {{PublisherType.regular}} – usual setup
### {{PublisherType.db}} – MQ DB publisher which publishes events to local DB and has a cron to send them to SNS transactionally for better delivery guarantees
# SQS only – they have {{""}} subscriber names ({{queue_name}} in the generator code)
## By shards
### Unsharded – usual setup
### Sharded – interesting use case, as basically application-level shards have to match in both producer and consumer, so that messages from all per-shard queues would be consumed

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
We technically support FIFO, but there isn’t a single usage of it yet 🤷‍♂️ 
{panel}

Code-level stats aren’t going to give much information though, they would become much more valuable if we combined them with the actual usage (traffic + cost) of different categories of setups.

Hi [~accountid:712020:0b672045-ccee-47bd-a209-1bec8346b45c] - as discussed over Slack, I see that EY is still refusing to agree to an indemnity, on the basis that such an indemnity would be “_unnecessary_” in light of the parties being independent controllers. This is not entirely correct.

*Reasoning*

It is true that, as independent controllers, Bolt and EY are individually accountable for their data protection compliance. However, this does not render data protection indemnities between the parties as “unnecessary”. 
If, for example, an error in EY’s systems resulted in the personal data at-issue being the subject of a data breach, it is possible that a disgruntled Romanian employee could pursue action against Bolt (being the entity most readily available to the employee) for failing to keep their personal data safe. In such circumstances, it would be reasonable for Bolt to expect to be reimbursed for any financial losses Bolt incurred as a result of EY’s systems error.
As such, it is still important for us to ensure that Bolt is properly contractually protected.

However, I note that EY seems unlikely to budge on this position, and that this issue is the final blocker towards pushing ahead with the agreement. As such, in the circumstances, we can take the following approach:

# I will write back to EY myself one more time to explain why we require an indemnity, and why we think the mutual indemnity proposed is a fair middle ground.
# If EY continues to refuse to accept any sort of indemnity, then we can take a risk-based approach and proceed with the DSA as currently agreed (i.e., without the indemnity) / push ahead with the agreement. 

*Reasoning*

As previously explained, proceeding without any sort of indemnity is the least-preferred approach from the Privacy side (as it does the least to protect Bolt’s position from a contractual perspective, particularly if non-compliance by EY leads to any action against Bolt).
However, I note the following from the proposed arrangement:
* The work at issue is discrete and is is not an indeterminate relationship / is unlikely to last longer than 2 years
* EY is already likely to have robust security measures in place.
* The personal data to be shared with EY is the names, contact details, salaries and positions of Romanian employees. Though higher risk, this does not amount to EY having _unlimited_ access to Bolt’s systems.
* EY has otherwise agreed to our DSA and the security obligations contained therein.
In such circumstances, if EY will not budge on the indemnity point, then it is open to the business to go ahead without it, provided that it accepts the liability risk here.

I will email EY shortly. Let me know if you have any questions 🙂

hey [~accountid:6071993aef87dd006894d4bd] 

The difference between the personal data and sensitive data (that includes special categories of data) is the following:

* By personal data we usually mean the data that identifies the individual directly (like name, ID, phone number) or indirectly (if linked to direct data like age or sex or other data that indirectly cannot identify the individual unless linked to the direct identifiers). Just personal data usually does not pose a high risk as sensitive data does.
** *Personal data includes:*
*** Name
*** Email address
*** Phone number
*** Date of birth
*** Photos of an individual face or orders
*** Order history
*** Restaurant ordered
*** Other data that does not fall into sensitive categories below
* *Sensitive data includes*
** *Special categories of data defined under the GDPR*
*** Racial or ethnic origin
*** Political opinions
*** Religious or philosophical beliefs
*** Trade union membership
*** Genetic data
*** Biometric data (when used for identification purposes, like fingerprints or facial recognition)
*** Health data (including mental and physical health information, medical books)
*** Sexual orientation or sex life information
** *Other data that is considered sensitive due to its nature and risk*
*** Identification numbers (e.g., social security numbers, passport numbers)
*** Location data (e.g., home or delivery address, IP address)
*** Payment information (payment method used, bank info, IBAN)
*** Information about children up to 16 y.o.
*** Photos that contains the information above or naked body parts of an individual

Hi all - jumping in on this from the privacy side.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*In summary:*

* Re whether we can block the driver, I defer to GFT on this issue, but I would flag that we need to first assess whether there has been a breach of the T&Cs / whether we can take action against drivers in such circumstances.
* Re obliging drivers to register cameras in our app / sending notifications / using stickers, I would +*not*+ recommend pursuing these options from a Privacy POV because:
** Obliging drivers to take any steps in this regard poses both privacy and reclass risks; and
** There is currently a global project in the pipeline regarding dashcams/CCTV in cars, which will cover a few of these issues, and we should avoid implementing ad hoc solutions that could undermine the project. 
* Instead, for the present case, we can remind the driver to comply with applicable laws. However, I am keen to hear the wider team’s views on this.
{panel}

I include further context on the reasoning below, if helpful.

*Blocking the driver*

This is less of a privacy issue and more for GFT to comment on.
Nevertheless, we need to be careful with what grounds we are relying on when we choose to block users, in case this results in any further escalation down the road. As such, we should check whether the driver’s behaviour violates our T&Cs and what action we are entitled to take against the driver, just to make sure that our bases are covered should we decide to block.

*Demanding that drivers register their cameras in the Bolt app*

From a privacy POV, we have taken the position that drivers are independent controllers of any footage recorded on their dashcams - this position allows us to sidestep a lot of privacy law issues that would otherwise arise, and is one we recently reiterated to the Estonian regulator. In order to be able to maintain this position, *we need to be able to demonstrate that we do not exercise any control over the use of the cameras*. Similarly, to avoid dashcams being regarded as ‘work equipment’ (which raises reclass issues), we need to make sure that we are not seen as exercising any sort of control over the cameras / enforcing that drivers use them. Although requiring drivers to register cameras that they independently own is a step away from this, it still flirts with the same issues (i.e., *this could be interpreted as Bolt trying to exercise a form of control, which we need to try and avoid*).
It is worth noting that Uber previously took this approach in 2023 (see [here|https://www.uber.com/en-GB/blog/london/register-your-dashcam/#:~:text=Uber%20will%20notify%20riders%20if,trip%20with%20a%20different%20driver.]), but made it _voluntary_ for drivers to register the dashcam. This could be a way of mitigating some of the above risks, but IMO *it would not solve the present issue* (i.e., the present driver could simply avid registering their camera).
As such, for both legal risk reasons and reasons of practicality, *I would not recommend this option*.

*Sending in-app notifications / requiring drivers to use stickers*

See the above points regarding privacy issues / reclass risk, which also apply here - *we need to avoid exercising control over the driver’s use of the dashcam*, and requiring drivers to use stickers could amount to this.
It is also worth noting that Antoni Wende and Sarra Eddahiri will be working on a global project regarding dashcams/CCTV in cars, which is currently in the pipeline (it does not appear to be in Q4 MVRA). This project will cover information obligations, as well as in-app notifications, and Privacy will be working with Product Legal and GFT on it. Ideally, we want to *avoid implementing ad hoc solutions before this project has been completed*, in case this causes any complications to the project further down the road.
As such, *I would not recommend either of these options for now from a Privacy POV*.

*Other possible solutions*

In light of the above, one proposed step would be to *remind drivers like this one to comply with applicable laws* - this way, we are not exercising control over the driver’s use of the dashcam, but at least we are nudging them in the right direction and potentially discouraging them.
Nevertheless, I appreciate that this option is not a ‘gleaming fix-all solution’, and sp I am keen to hear the wider team’s views for other potential angles.

Bolt in cooperation with ETH will collect the following data.

*How:*

The Lab will utilize special instrumentation, conduct field work and extensive data collection and processing, including:

For two cities - Malaga ES and Oldenburg DE:

* 20 e-scooters instrumented with acceleration, microclimate and overtaking sensors. The measurements wills be taken for at least 6 months to capture season and non-summer seasons.  
* Travel surveys including tourists and locals during the summer 2025
* Questionnaires through Bolt’s app after rides

In addition:

* There is a possibility that the fleet of scooters deployed for this project will be the Bolt 6.0 model equipped with onboard cameras.

Data points - in addition to what [~accountid:712020:61ed0b58-3168-4847-8428-1f7d24c05b13] wrote:

* Historical Bolt ridership data - electric scooters (Malaga and Oldenburg) and ride hailing (Malaga).
* Scope of data collection proposed by ETH Zurich for the project with Bolt:

** We will focus on changes in the amount of ridership, location of ridership, equity issues surrounding ridership, and ridership characteristics (duration, speed, etc) derived from the implementation of concepts. 
** This task will focus on evaluating safety by analysing historical accident/crash records, acceleration patterns of micromobility vehicles and the proximity of overtaking vehicles. It will offer a comprehensive understanding of the risks faced by e-scooter and e-bike riders to evaluate improvements in safety through infrastructure redesign. 
** Acceleration data, collected through onboard sensors (10 sensors), will be used to detect abrupt changes in speed, which may indicate hazardous situations such as sudden braking, swerving to avoid obstacles, or collisions. By comparing acceleration profiles across different areas and conditions, we can identify specific locations or scenarios where riders are more likely to encounter safety issues. Contextual data on road conditions, weather, and traffic density will be collected, when available, to understand how these factors influence acceleration patterns. Overtaking distance sensors (10 sensors), on the other hand, will measure the space between micromobility users and passing vehicles. Close overtakes are a significant risk factor for e-scooter and e-bike riders, as they increase the likelihood of accidents. By analysing the data from these sensors, we can assess the frequency and severity of close passes in different contexts, such as varying road types, traffic conditions, and the presence of dedicated bike lanes. Micromobility users will be encouraged to report hazardous situations through Bolt’s app to provide additional context and validation for sensor-based findings. 
** Accident/crash likelihood will be estimated, informed by the data collected with the onboard sensors, and will be compared to historical crash statistics. The link between close passes, hazardous situations, and observed crash risk will be defined. Once the link is established, a few hazardous areas will be monitored more closely to collect traffic count data. Fieldwork will be carried out to get a detailed understanding of the infrastructure conditions in these hazardous areas. Infrastructure modifications for these areas will be proposed and assessed based on the modelling of future traffic flows and identified correlations between infrastructure conditions and safety. Potentially, some infrastructure modifications (e.g., dedicated lanes with physical separation, speed bumps, curb extensions) can be implemented during the pilot phase of the lab and the change in high-risk situations identified by the sensors will be re-evaluated. This will enable us to measure the impacts of infrastructure re-design on the crash risk experienced by riders. 
** *_Urban heat effects and cooling measures for increased micromobility use and walkability (Lead: TMP)._*  
** This task will focus on studying the user behaviour related to temperature and microclimate. As differences in ridership exist between seasons, it is essential to fully understand the differences between the different riders. We will use the available data to correlate the travel behaviour of pedestrians, micromobility and ride-sharing users with meteorological variables such as air temperature, precipitation, and relative humidity. Following this, we will carry out a more detailed modelling of the microclimate—considering factors such as air temperature, relative humidity, mean radiant temperature, and wind speed—at the smallest possible scale (at least a 10-metre grid, depending on data availability). This will allow the connection of microclimate conditions with the specific routes taken by pedestrians and micromobility users, enabling us to assess the impact of microclimate on users' thermal comfort during their trips. Microclimate sensors (10 sensors) will be installed on e-scooters/e-bikes to measure temperature and humidity. A differentiation between locals and tourists will be carried out as tourists usually come from colder regions and therefore might evaluate the microclimate conditions differently. Based on the analysis of users' thermal comfort, urban heat hotspots will be identified and cooling measures will be proposed.  
** In addition to microclimate data, we will incorporate route-specific attributes, such as the type of road infrastructure (e.g., bike lanes, primary roads, sidewalks), the number of intersections and the infrastructure surroundings (e.g., open spaces, building density, greenery) to identify which route characteristics are most preferred by users. These insights will be further validated through post-trip questionnaires integrated into Bolt’s app, ensuring that the findings derived from tracked data are confirmed by user feedback.

Whenever when amending the non-compete, our protection for this decreases and in this case, it’s a consultant which I understand operates with these kinds of services with competitors. However, if you deem that the current clauses are OK from a commercial point of view, then all good from my end. To provide some background, please see below in relation to certain of the more important changes made:

* *Definition of Competing Business*:
** To mitigate the Consultant’s wish and our needs I have now linked the *definition to the type of work specified in the SoW*. With this being done, I think it’s fine to keep the non-compete clauses as is, without further additions. This means any territorial clauses are still valid (hence the addition in the SoW to include “e.g.” Norway).
* *Clause 6.3 regarding delayed payments:*
** As for the Consultant’s wish to include that any delayed payments of more than 7 days shall be deemed as a material breach in respect of clause 3.2.1 I would instead propose either of the following alternatives. 
*** 1) Include a late interest payment which would be counted from the day after the due date; or
*** 2) Raise the number of days from 7 days to 20 days. 
*** Please note that accounting should be aware that payments of this specific agreement really must be done in due time.
* *Clause 12.1 regarding limitation of liability*:
** Although the Consultant wants to exclude 12.1 (b)-(d) I think that we should keep this, as damages in relation to breaches for these clauses are generally of such kind that they result in high damages. Therefore, capping such under a liability clause, is generally really not favourable for us.
* *Clause 12.5 regarding maximum aggregate liability*:
** I have amended this clause as to reflect incurred fees as to compromise with the Consultant on this point. However, as you mentioned, the cap of NOK 400,000 will very quickly become too low as a cap for this agreement, considering that you anticipate work for NOK 110,000 per month and that the Consultant should at least work four months. If they really do want an alternative cap with an amount, this should be higher.
* *Use of “Bolt’s sole/absolute” discretion”*:
** The above is used in relation to clause 2.3 as well as clause 4.1.8, please see a few comments in relation to these:
*** *2.3* - As Bolt is the entity ordering of the Services it is reasonable that any deviations/breaches of the Services provided are due to Bolt’s discretion to decide. However, in order to facilitate the wish of the Consultant I propose adding an addition, according to which Bolt shall inform the Consultant of such deviation/breach, wherever the parties can discuss and the Consultant will have e.g. 7 days for remedy. 
*** *4.1.8* - As this clause is corresponding to clause 3.2.4 giving us the possibility to terminate the Agreement with immediate effect, I would rather change the wording “at Bolt’s sole discretion” to “In Bolt’s reasonable opinion” instead of as in clause 2.3 include a way to remedy this. ** *_Why is it important to keep this fixed payment regardless of the no. of rides performed?_* Paying the drivers for promoting the Bolt brand even if they do not perform any rides for Bolt is a major mitigation action to reduce the reclassification risk. If the driver gets paid only if they perform rides, it could be argued that Bolt incentives financially the drivers to opt for it and to work mainly for its platform, putting drivers in a position of dependency, which could be considered by judges as a clue characterizing an employment relationship between the driver and Bolt.  
** Nature of the branding services: branding the cars does not mean wearing a uniform. branding is an advertising service provided by the Driver.→  Please note that branding services are separate advertising services rendered by the driver. Although we  can structure the fees for the ad services to include a variable part that will increase based on the visibility given to the logo (ie kickback commission) we need to ensure a fixed payment for the service provided as it would be requested by any professional advertising service agreement (“agence media”).

If you can confirm the above, I believe that the risk assessment doesn’t changes significantly and we are good to go.

However, I would like to review the screens and the communication sent to drivers to make sure they align to our standard narrative and guidelines.

Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, the law requires a data controller such as ourselves to protect the rights of third parties (in particular, the rights of passengers). Furthermore, we must point out that we are not required to disclose documents or otherwise provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

We will share copies of the personal data we hold about you to which you are entitled, in particular your trip history on 3 August 2024. Please note that we have redacted certain information to protect the rights of passengers.

* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

*Your rights* 

You have the right to request rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing of personal data concerning you or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You have the right to complain directly to the appropriate supervisory authority and seek a judicial remedy. 

If you have any additional questions, please let us know.

Yours sincerely,

The first question is a bit ambiguous - you can operate a vehicle if your ID card is not valid. You cannot operate a motor vehicle if your driver’s license is expired. 

At the moment we are (by default) enforcing the limitations on people with visas and/or temporary residency permits. This means, that once your permit(s) expire, you cannot render services on Bolt platform anymore. 

§ 43 [https://www.riigiteataja.ee/en/eli/508072024002/consolide|https://www.riigiteataja.ee/en/eli/508072024002/consolide|smart-link]  specifies the grounds for working.

 _(2) A vehicle card can be applied for a power-driven vehicle that has been entered in the motor register and complies with the requirements arising from this Act. In addition to the document specified in clause 1 of subsection 1 or clause 1 of subsection 3 of this section, the applicant for a vehicle card must submit the following to the issuer of the vehicle card:_

# _the contract of use of the vehicle where the applicant is not the owner of the vehicle or a user of the vehicle specified in the registration certificate;_

Hey, [~accountid:62b2cf3c0c77011bdfdcdbcd]! There are a few considerations to keep in mind. I used guidance provided by Product Legal here: [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C040NCWV75H/p1722514865864119|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C040NCWV75H/p1722514865864119|smart-link] and [https://docs.google.com/document/d/19gQTYP1qwPrSi33ZZYcuryKGNxQ4oCd2JGMhW7_ohDY/edit|https://docs.google.com/document/d/19gQTYP1qwPrSi33ZZYcuryKGNxQ4oCd2JGMhW7_ohDY/edit|smart-link].

To conduct the assessment you need to know: 

# What is the risk level of your market (SK) - info is here: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1eLfh8fqZVri-ffJUhfPQKdkwFoKRQJDlRed5SkGM1Lc/edit?gid=1690906916#gid=1690906916|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1eLfh8fqZVri-ffJUhfPQKdkwFoKRQJDlRed5SkGM1Lc/edit?gid=1690906916#gid=1690906916|smart-link].
# Whether in your market rh services are provided by fleets, individual drivers or both - you can ask from ops in the ticket or reach out to someone from RH team directly.
# What external benefits will be provided? You can ask from ops in the ticket.
# What internal benefits will be provided? You can ask from ops in the ticket.

Based on the reclassification risk level of the market and type of providers of transportation services (fleets - lower risk, individual drivers - higher risk) you can assess whether external and internal benefits increase risk of reclassification. 

General advice: avoid automatic enrolment to the programme, use number of finished rides as a metric, provide benefits of low value, avoid internal benefits that look like employer’s benefits. At the moment the following internal benefits are considered high risk and should be avoided: See price and destination and Driver Queue Optimisation.

For more details and inspiration, please see this RO ticket: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-38509|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-38509|smart-link]

2QA: General theme for this issue is how calls are behaving when app is killed/for long time in background and/or user got logged out. Following scenarios are worth testing:
1. App (rider or driver) is killed and opposite party is calling. Call should work normally with correct Caller name.
2. App (rider or driver) is in background for longer than 30s and opposite party is calling. Call should work normally with correct Caller name.
3. As described in ticket, driver is logged in, had order with rider in the past (so rider can call him from call history). App is killed on Device A, he logs into Device B. Then rider calls him. 
**Expected output**: Call works fine on Device B. There's **no** crash log generated on Device A (you can look for that locally in Settings->Privacy&Security->Analytics&Improvments->Analytics Data->Search for Bolt Prelive) from the time of testing.
4. Same as in point 3 but this time, Rider is getting logged out from his device. I'm not sure how QA can simulate such case (as riders, opposed to drivers, can be logged in in multiple devices) but maybe you know some tricks?

Thank you for escalating to Customer Payments team. The customers don't always have a great visibility when the pre-authorization has been returned to them. Returning the pre-authorization is not something Bolt has much control over. 
Depending on the bank the pre-authorization charges can take up to a month to be returned to the customer. 
If the Authorization state is Captured then everything is fine on our side and the customer has to check with their bank. 

Please only escalate the issue to Payment Operations team if

1. The funds have not been returned after 30 days and customer has checked with their bank

2. The state has been stuck in authorization for more than 24 hours. (72h for Micro Mobility) 

3. The state of the authorization is failed or error. 

Please leave a comment on the ticket if you still want it to be escalated to the Customer Payments team. Else the ticket will be closed in 5 days.

Hi team, 
Thank you for escalating to Customer Payments team. The customers don't always have a great visibility when the pre-authorization has been returned to them. Returning the pre-authorization is not something Bolt has much control over. 
Depending on the bank the pre-authorization charges can take up to a month to be returned to the customer. 
If the Authorization state is Captured then everything is fine on our side and the customer has to check with their bank. 

Please only escalate the issue to Payment Operations team if

1. The funds have not been returned after 30 days and customer has checked with their bank

2. The state has been stuck in authorization for more than 24 hours. (72h for Micro Mobility) 

3. The state of the authorization is failed or error. 

Please leave a comment on the ticket if you still want it to be escalated to the Customer Payments team. Else the ticket will be closed in 5 days.

The user is reporting an incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. TLDR from Dragonfly evaluation:

* performance is comparable with Redis+Search module.
* Dragonfly also doing pretty long recovery during cold restart, same as Redis search
* It's faster with more cores, but since we cannot use it in cluster mode, we have to use master/replica mode with quite big nodes, which are more expensive than current cluster and will have longer maintenance
* SSD mode with quick testing doesn't look stable and doesn't work at all, will probably test from scratch later
* Dragonfly will inevitably have diff with Search module in terms of search results/etc
* So with less flexibility there's no much improvements comparing with plain Redis+Search module and we agreed to continue testing user-embeddings cluster with Redis+Search.

I checked also GH issues of the project and found some "not great, not terrible" stuff, like:
* Noeviction mode, which is enabled by default, actually accepts keys for write when full, but drops them. Redis in comparison, throws errors in same scenario and Profiling clusters use this to avoid re-provisioning profiles when Redis has outage/full, https://github.com/dragonflydb/dragonfly/issues/2984
* High latency on snapshots https://github.com/dragonflydb/dragonfly/issues/2389
* Master freeze on replica freeze https://github.com/dragonflydb/dragonfly/issues/2191
* OOM even with cache-mode=true https://github.com/dragonflydb/dragonfly/issues/3155

{quote}_Hi Shahana,_

_In_ [_@Karmel Kristin Einberg_|mailto:karmel.einberg@bolt.eu]_'s absence, I have been looking into this._

_However, I did come across the_ *_2019 Loi d'Orientation des Mobilités (LOM) – Mobility Law_*_._

_Doing my own research, this seems more relevant to us as it requires platforms in the transport and delivery sectors to:_

* _Establish a framework for social dialogue between platforms and gig workers, allowing negotiation of working conditions without necessarily reclassifying workers as employees._
* _Offer certain social protections, particularly accident insurance, to gig workers._
* _Increase transparency regarding how earnings are calculated, working conditions, and the consequences of task refusal or cancellation._

_However, I could not find any required annuity in the LOM Law, nor is there a specific minimum amount that needs to be provided for accident insurance._

_Therefore, I would be interested to see what either Marsh or any of the insurers have discovered on this topic._ {quote}

Sorry, I have just been catching up on emails, and Marsh has given some guidance on this topic. Email attached and excerpt below:

{quote}Hi Dan,  

 

Please find below a summary of information we have gathered from our team regarding the El Khomri law.

We would like to clarify that this is not our legal advice. This summary reflects Marsh’s perspective on insurance products related to the law. To ensure compliance, we strongly recommend that Bolt consult and validate this information with your legal counsel.

 

------------------------------------------------------------

 

_The El Khomri law amended_ +_the labor code_+ _on many points,_ +_including the coverage of independent workers against work-related accidents._+

_The Social Security Code has also been modified to provide for a voluntary membership system for this insurance for individuals who do not benefit from the general social protection scheme._

 

_The Article L7342-2 of the labor code provides for two scenarios, to protect independent workers:_

* _Either the worker subscribes on their own and the platform reimburses them (up to a ceiling set by decree)_

* _Or the worker joins a collective contract subscribed by the platform._

 

_When an independent worker subscribes to insurance covering the risk of work-related accidents or joins the “voluntary insurance” (related to the labor code) for work-related accidents mentioned in Article L. 743-1 of the Social Security Code, the platform must reimburse the premium, up to a limit set by decree. This limit cannot exceed the contribution provided for in the same Article L. 743-1._

_This first paragraph of this article does not apply when the worker joins a collective contract subscribed by the platform that includes guarantees at least equivalent to the voluntary insurance for work-related accidents mentioned in the first paragraph, and the contribution to this contract is covered by the platform._

                                   

_Therefore, the El Khomri Law requires that life insurance contracts of platforms be at least equivalent to the “voluntary insurance”, which includes the following provisions:_

+_Payment of a capital or disability annuity_++-_:_-+

* *_Depending on the consequences of the work-related accident or occupational disease, a rate of disability may be assigned. The insured is then entitled to:_*

# _A capital payment if the rate is less than 10%_
# _A disability annuity until retirement age if the rate of IPP is equal to or greater than 10%_

 

+_Reimbursement of funeral expenses and payment of a capital to beneficiaries in case of death:_+

* *_In the event of the insured's death resulting from a work-related accident or occupational disease:_*

# _Funeral expenses and, if applicable, transportation expenses of the body to the place of burial, are reimbursed, upon presentation of supporting documents, to the person who paid them, up to the limit of the expenses incurred, with a maximum amount set at €1,932.00 as of January 1, 2024. This person can be a close relative of the deceased insured (spouse, partner bound by a civil solidarity pact, cohabitant, ascendant, descendant, heir, friend, etc.) or a third party (funeral home, etc.)._
# _Capital to their beneficiaries._

 

[_Chapitre II : Responsabilité sociale des plateformes (Articles L7342-1 à L7342-11) - Légifrance (legifrance.gouv.fr)_|https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/codes/section_lc/LEGITEXT000006072050/LEGISCTA000033013020/]

 

------------------------------------------------------------

 

For fleet partners, our understanding is that Bolt’s fleet partners are companies that supply their own vehicles and employ drivers directly. As a result, these companies are responsible for providing “voluntary insurance” (social insurance) for their employees. Please could you confirm that our understanding here is accurate?

If it is, depending on the cost of the voluntary insurance for independent workers, we could suggest that Bolt continues to provide personal accident coverage (PA) for the employees of these fleet partners.

 

Thereby, our recommendation would be to explore the possibility of a blanket insurance policy covering all drivers. This would reduce premiums through volume and risk sharing, while also simplifying operational management and costs with verifying individual drivers insurance.

 

Please feel free to reach out if you have any further questions.

 

Many thanks and best regards,

Shahana

 

*Shahana Vibisnaa*

Project Manager,

+*INTERNAL UPDATE ON THE FACTS*+

* The rider [complained|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/385665072] to Bolt about the trip at 14:57 on 1 June. Bolt passed the complaint on to the driver at 16:52 on the same day, [notifying|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/385723321] the driver that “_I am writing regarding a report made about you concerning a trip you had on 1/06/2024. We received a report from the passenger that stated that you allegedly asked for cash for an in-app payment trip. We ask you to avoid asking cash for an in-app order, If the passenger has a pet_”. 
** IMO, the driver could use this to figure out which rider made the complaint. Indeed, we have proof that the driver did figure this out, as they replied to Bolt “_Thats a lie. She asked me if u wanna take tip in cash or card._”
* Before complaining about the driver calling the rider, the rider was complaining to Bolt about not being refunded the cash tip that they were allegedly forced to give the driver. This continued until 19:58 on 1 June, at which point the rider complained about being called by the driver.
** At 20:28, Bolt Safety Team [reached out|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/385856585] to the driver saying “_We received a report from the driver that stated that you allegedly tried contacting and yelling at the passenger after the ride. We would like to believe that this is not a common occurrence and it was simply a misunderstanding. However, this report, while inconclusive at this time, may be used as a reference in the future should something similar occur again. This is not to assume guilt, but just for safety precautions_”. This effectively closed the issue on the driver side.
* At 20:44, the rider included “_a screenshot of the call_” - this is the screenshot of the landline number provided to us by the ICO. According to the screenshot, the call occurred at 19:57.
* The phone number included in the screenshot is not associated (and was never associated) the the driver’s account, and could not have been in any event, given that it is a landline number.
** Given that phone masking is on in the UK, the driver’s (landline) phone number would not have been visible to the rider upon calling them (and vice-versa). As such, the rider should not have access to the driver’s landline number in a screenshot, if they were called through the app.

+*CONCLUSION*+

Perhaps we are incorrect in our assumption that the landline number in the screenshot belongs to the driver - in any event, it seems like the obvious next step is to confirm a few points with the rider.

* The rider asserts that the number in the screenshot is the number they were called from by the driver. However, this should not be possible according to internal investigations.
* Given that the rider was called within 24 hours of the trip finishing, this would be possible through in-app functionality. However, due to phone masking, neither user’s phone number should be visible to the other.
* Subject to further fact-finding, what I imagine happened here is as follows:
** (1) Rider complains to Bolt with specific complaint relating to pets / driver taking cash.
** (2) Driver is promptly notified about the complaint.
** (3) Based on the fact pattern, driver is able to ‘put two and two together’ and figure out which rider issued the complaint.
** (4) Driver calls the rider using Bolt’s in-app functionality and berates them.
** (5) Rider interprets this as driver having their phone number, as the call was received through their phone.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

We need to clarify a few factual points with the rider, as the above theory seems to be the only one that is possible. If the rider is able to confirm: (a) that the landline phone number is not the driver’s; and (b) the rider was called through the app, then we can explain the situation and hopefully nip this complaint in the bud.

* _Through clause 3.5. and clause 9, paragraph 1, (a), Bolt may terminate the agreement at any time with immediate effect if the fleet commits any serious or repeated breach or fails to observe any of the provisions of the agreement or refuses or neglects to comply with any reasonable and lawful directions of Bolt_
* _Given the fleet’s failure to comply with the KPIs, Bolt may terminate the agreement and claim a compensation for the costs incurred and for the damages resulting from fleet’s breach of its obligations._
* _it is advisable to send a termination letter with acknowledgment of receipt, justifying the termination and claiming damages i.e. requesting the payment of penalties and/or advance payment pro rata for the remaining months. Considering the term of the Agreements, the months of breach of KPI and the remaining months until the end of the contracts it is reasonable to terminate with immediate effect without a cure period._ 
* _The purpose of this Agreement was for Bolt to promote growth of sales by further incentivizing selected partners through an advanced “cash-back” bonus subject to performance objectives in a target period in the Portuguese territory, so it is arguable that the purpose has failed and the advance payment for KPI not fulfilled should be returned._
* _In case one of the Contracts contests the termination and does not voluntarily pay the claimed amount (or, in this case, returns the Fee or remaining pro rata Fee), and Bolt intends to judicial recover it, it should be noted that, with regard to the request for payment for the remaining months of the Agreement, this claim may pose some challenges as it can understood by the Courts as an abusive exercise of the right of termination, since these “penalties” are being demanded in advance and without the possibility of the Fleet fulfilling the KPI's for the remaining months of the initial duration of the contract. Thus, there is a possibility that the Court will reject a claim for the payment of the remaining advance payment following termination._
* _This reasoning does not apply to the contractual penalties provided for in Clause 3.5 which are already due at the time of termination (i.e. the penalties applied during the term of the Agreement), and for which payment would be due regardless of whether the contract was terminated before its expiry date._
* _Therefore, it seems to us that there is a risk that the courts may consider that the amount already paid by Bolt for each vehicle may not be fully recovered._



+In sum, DLA considers that Bolt can terminate both agreements and request (i) the payment of the remaining months (notwithstanding the fragilities identified above) and also (ii) the contractual penalty.+

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.

* the fraud policy is approached from a human perspective - ensuring fairness in all cases (e.g. no case will turn red after first occasion);
* we may face complaints from consumer protection authorities and in such cases, we could be required to disclose the fraud policy, change the fraud policy and issue refunds to customers who complained;
* a better refund policy is shared with us after the tests in Q4 for our revision as the current Excel sheet is very vague/incomprehensible.

Regarding your first point, could you please clarify whether you’re referring to all fraud rules or just the profiling rules? We can certainly exclude cases where users have zero refund history, but doing so might undermine the core purpose of the profiling rules. Their main objective is to identify refund abusers who cannot be easily flagged by CS agents/human perspective. Fraudsters often create brand new accounts with no prior history, making it difficult to determine whether their first refund request is legitimate. However, profiling data can help us tackle this challenge. For instance, if we detect that more than two accounts were created with the same IP and the refund ratio for these accounts exceeds 50% of the order value, it raises suspicion.


That said, we are always prepared to adjust or revert our rules based on testing outcomes or if complaints arise from authorities.

By way of update on this - I spoke with the ‘dev-comms’ team who have confirmed that the number that called the rider ([+441628904101|tel:+441628904101], as included in the screenshot) is a Bolt phone masking number. As such, +*neither the rider nor the driver here has access to the other’s phone number*+. Instead, it appears that what happened here was as follows:

* At 14:57 on 1 June, the rider [complained|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/385665072] to Bolt that the driver had asked for a cash tip.
* At 16:52, Bolt reached out to the driver [notifying|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/385723321] them that “_I am writing regarding a report made about you concerning a trip you had on 1/06/2024. We received a report from the passenger that stated that you allegedly asked for cash for an in-app payment trip. We ask you to avoid asking cash for an in-app order, If the passenger has a pet_”. The driver was clearly able to associate this report with a passenger (particularly given its specificity), as the driver responded “_Thats a lie. She asked me if u wanna take tip in cash or card._”
* As 24 hours had not passed since the trip, at 19:57 the driver was able to call with rider using the Bolt phone masking number. From the rider’s perspective, this _looked like_ the driver had their mobile number and was calling from the driver’s landline, whereas in reality this call was made through the phone masking functionality.
* After 24 hours expired, the driver was no longer able to contact the rider.

This is good news, as it means that we have a good story to tell. To close this out properly, I recommend that we send three messages: (1) one to the driver; (2) one to the rider; and (3) one to the ICO. Drafts on each are below.

*RATIONALE*: 
The ICO has requested that “_Appropriate steps are taken to address this with the driver in question_”. We would like to believe that this is not a common occurrence and it was simply a misunderstanding. However, this report, while inconclusive at this time, may be used as a reference in the future should something similar occur again. This is not to assume guilt, but just for safety precautions_”, and can flag this to the ICO. 
However, to fully close this off, IMO we should send an additional message to the driver encouraging them not to do this sort of thing in the future. Results of the scond test with frozen locks and centerpunch:

*OKAI ES600 - Battery Lock Winterization (Second Test - Center Punch Method)*

Test Overview:

* Number of battery locks tested: 9
* Freezing temperature: -24°C
* Duration in freezing conditions: 3 days

Each battery lock was subjected to different conditions, with some treated and others left untreated. Below are the results:



*_Untreated Locks (Samples 1 to 6):_*

# *Battery Lock Control Test 1 (Untreated, Simulated Condensation)*

Condition: Soaked in hot water to simulate condensation.

Result: After 8 attempts with the center punch method, the lock started working but failed again after 5 minutes. After 3 more attempts, it resumed functioning.

# *Battery Lock Control Test 2 (Untreated, Simulated Condensation)*

Condition: Soaked in hot water to simulate condensation.

Result: The lock started working after 12 attempts but failed again for 30 minutes before becoming functional.

# *Battery Lock Control Test 3 (Untreated, Extreme Test)*

Condition: Soaked in hot salty water to maintain freezing conditions.

Result: The lock worked briefly after 10 attempts but stopped permanently after.

# *Battery Lock Control Test 4 (Untreated, Extreme Test)*

Condition: Soaked in hot salty water to maintain freezing conditions.

Result: The lock never worked, even after 20 attempts.

# *Battery Lock Control Test 5 (Untreated, Dry)*

Condition: Dry.

Result: The lock worked after 9 attempts with no further issues.

# *Battery Lock Control Test 6 (Untreated, Dry)*

Condition: Dry.

Result: The lock worked after 6 attempts but stopped. It resumed working after 4 more attempts.



*_Treated Locks (Samples 7 to 10):_*

# *Battery Lock Extreme Test 7 (Treated with Injected Lithium Grease, Extreme Test)*

Condition: Soaked in hot salty water.

Result: Did not work on the first attempt, but after using the center punch, it started working and continued without any issues.

# *Battery Lock Test 8 (Treated with Lithium Spray, Simulated Condensation)*

Condition: Soaked in hot water to simulate condensation.

Result: Did not work on the first attempt. After 3 attempts with the center punch, the lock started working but briefly stopped. After 2 more attempts, it resumed functioning.

# *Battery Lock Test 9 (Treated with Injected Lithium Grease, Dry)*

Condition: Dry.

Result: Worked on the first attempt with no further issues.

# *Battery Lock Test 10 (Treated with Lithium Spray, Dry)*

Condition: Dry.

Result: Did not work on the first attempt, but after using the center punch, it worked on the second attempt with no further issues.



*Conclusions:* 

* The treated locks, especially those injected with lithium grease, performed significantly better under freezing conditions compared to untreated ones.
* Treating the locks with lithium and using the center punch as a last resort is, without a doubt, the most effective strategy for combating harsh winter conditions on the streets.
